commits.subject: Answer as an expert in whatever the question is about

body.text: The one instruction in this brief to be clever rather than careful, and it earns its place: the person answering cannot add the sentence the machine left out, every correction costing them a letter at a time — so a vague or hedged answer is not a starting point they can improve, it is the whole of what they get to say.
Bounded twice, because an expert tone is the other half of the risk here:

items: Knowing the subject is not talking like one. Still two sentences of the plain words they would have used, and never a lecture.
Expert in the subject, never about them. An expert tone is exactly what would make an invented claim about somebody believed, so the rule about whose facts these are is restated on the same line.

commits.subject: Draw the answers from three sources, not the board alone

body.text: Told to offer the phrases that answer the question, a model with two thousand of them in front of it filled all twenty cells from the table: a board that size holds something loosely on topic for anything anybody ever asks, so the feature became a search of the board. What somebody is missing when they are asked something is usually the words they have not got.

items: The brief names three sources — their own phrases, answers the model writes in their voice, and answers out of what it looked up — and asks for them mixed through the list rather than grouped, since the first few cells are the ones a tired reader gets to.

Their own phrases are capped at a third of the list. `FROM_BOARD_CAP` enforces it in `mixed`, because a brief is a request: the overflow is dropped rather than reordered, best-first being the model's judgement, so a list that ignores the brief is drawn shorter and says so.
The guide says where the answers come from.

commits.subject: Offer up to twenty answers on the board instead of one reply

body.text: A question used to be answered with a single reply written into the message box: a stranger's sentence to accept or start again from by spelling. It is now up to twenty answers as cells on the board, under a pinned Answers tab — the surface somebody already chooses everything else from — and the one they rest on is a choice they made.

items: A suggestion is still never spoken. Choosing one puts it in the message box through the composer's own history; it is said on Speak, like any message. That now holds against auto-speak twice over: the answers arriving, and the dwell that chooses one — a gaze resting on a cell is how somebody reads it.
The answers are ordinary phrases, so a gap is the board's own blank: drawn dashed on the cell, and the caret lands in it when the answer is chosen.
The board goes to them as they are asked for and back to the tab it was on afterwards, holding the dwells across both moves.
A typed word does not narrow them; choosing one leaves the others up.
What is remembered of the exchange is the answer they took, not the one the model put first, and nothing at all where they answered off their own board.
The waiting line moved out of the message box onto the tab the answers land on, since nothing arrives in the box by itself any more.

commits.subject: Offer the board's own phrases first when suggesting a reply

body.text: Every phrase on the board, the emergency bar's included, now goes with the question, and the brief asks for one of them word for word wherever one answers it. The whole board rather than a keyword preselection, because what makes a phrase the answer is what it means.

items: The brief says the phrases are what the person can say, not facts about them, so a board holding "I'm in pain" is not read as evidence.
Slots with choices go as gaps, which land with the caret in them.
The board is cached for an hour, with the date after it.
It is sent in the board's own order, never the grid's usage order.
The Settings row, the guide and the privacy policy all say the board goes.

commits.subject: Keep the modes on the message box, fit the spinner labels, and write times in seconds

body.text: **The modes never sit left of the message box.** The strip is centred on the bar, where Rest is looked for without looking, and on a bar holding one box that centre is on the box. With the question beside the answer on a wide screen it is over the 2rem gap between the two, and edit sat on nothing. `left` is now the `max()` of the bar's centre and the place that puts the strip's left edge on the box's; the bar measures the two numbers that second place needs. Pushed only as far as it has to go rather than re-centred on the box — re-centring would move Rest a long way every time listen mode opened. Measured in a browser: centred at 640px with listen closed exactly as before, and nudged 22px to sit on the box's edge with it open. Unmeasured, it is the bar's centre, as it always was.

**The label beside a spinner is as wide as the widest thing it can say.** It was 32px whatever it held, which cut `1000ms` to `1000r` and ran `100%` into the + beside it. Sized to what it says now, it would move the + and the reset every time the value crossed a digit — and those are aimed at by position. So every value in range is written once and the widest drawn invisibly in the same grid cell, out of the text so a screen reader and a test read the value alone. And never narrower than a time, so the + lines up down the whole list: 576px on every row, measured.

**Every time in seconds, with three figures after the point or none.** The auto-repeat row said `1000ms` under two dwell rows saying `1.5s`. `1s`, `0.800s`, `1.050s` now — three because the repeat steps in fifty milliseconds and one figure would write `1050` as `1.1s`, a value it cannot hold. `seconds()` in `ui/units.ts`, used by all four time spinners across Settings and the sign-in page; the reset labels follow.

commits.subject: Size every icon on the message box like the microphone, on one grey ground

body.text: Every control riding either box's border is the microphone's size now — a 1.5rem control with a 1.2rem glyph in a quarter-rem of ground. Speak was a 3rem glyph and the heard box's tools 2.2rem circles, so the border read as things added one at a time rather than as one set. Speak is told apart by the accent and by being last in its row instead. The bar's top padding comes back to a rem, half the height of every strip on it.

Every one of them stands on the same ground, `--border-ground`: grey at fifteen per cent. The microphone, the modes, the actions, the slot that empties a box, the heard box's tools, the language and the voice, and the edit strip, whose category trigger takes the strip's ground rather than stacking a second on it.

Mixed into the bar rather than laid over it. A see-through fifteen per cent was tried first and let the box's border run straight through the glyphs — the focused box's green line crossing copy, paste and speak — which is exactly what these grounds were made solid to stop. This is the colour a fifteen-per-cent grey makes on the bar, but opaque.
`tests/app/App.test.tsx` holds every strip to the token and every glyph to the microphone's size.

commits.subject: Put every pane's scroll controls on its right, and draw a focused field once

body.text: **Scroll controls on the right.** `ScrollPane` put a bar of controls above its content and another below it; it has a rail down its right edge now, the grid's rail in every particular a gaze learns by — the same 44px, the same edge, the four sharing the height, the same fill rising from the bottom. One edge for everything that scrolls, and two strips of height back for a short screen. Every panel, picker, the sign-in page, the legal pages and the slot chooser take it from the one component.

The rail appears only while there is somewhere to go, so a pane that fits keeps its width — but then all four, always, the ones with nowhere to go inert in their place. They share the rail's height, and one that came and went would stretch the rest into its space under a resting pointer. The arrows inside the two text boxes follow the same rule now instead of leaving an empty slot.
The pane buttons carried a `.dwell-bar` that no rule ever animated, so holding one showed a tint and nothing counting down to the moment it fired. It rises from the bottom now, as the grid's does.
**Double borders in Settings.** Two:

items: Every focused field drew its own accent border and the app's focus ring three pixels outside it — every key, passphrase and figure a dwell had put the caret in. It was fixed on the message box alone. `.caret-field` takes the ring off too, and says focus on its own border.
The last setting's rule and the reset section's own rule sat forty-odd pixels apart with nothing between them. The reset keeps its space and loses its line.

body.text: Taking the ring off the heard box last time left it with no sign of focus at all, having never had a focus colour of its own; it has one. A guard now holds every field to both halves — no ring, and its own border — and found that the moment it was written.
Found by rendering Settings in a real browser and measuring every pair of border lines within a few pixels of each other, rather than by eye.

commits.subject: Make every grid wait for Done or Cancel (#76)

body.text: Choosing a spoken language closed the grid on the first tile a rest landed on, and its Cancel did exactly what Done did. The reply-model grid and the phrase-order grid did the same. On a board aimed at by gaze that is the wrong way round: a rest is how somebody looks at a tile as well as how they choose one, so a grid that commits to the first tile the eye passes over is choosing for them — and it left two buttons on screen that meant nothing.

`usePendingChoice` is the one rule for all three. A tile marks a choice, Done writes it, Cancel throws it away, and nothing about the board changes before one of them. It opens on what is chosen now rather than on what was last marked, so a grid cancelled out of and reopened does not arrive showing the choice it was told to forget.

The choice is held rather than applied and put back, because choosing a language writes down the voice it is leaving, and a language only passed over on the way to another must not leave a voice behind it. And Done with nothing moved writes nothing — not as an economy: the language the board is already in, chosen again, still writes the voice in use into the voice memory, and that settings change would travel to the other devices and arrive as "Board updated from your other device", a notice about something nobody did.
The voice picker keeps applying as it goes and putting back on Cancel, deliberately: every voice speaks as it is chosen, and hearing it is the point. The category picker already waited.

The phrase-order grid closing on the first tile was a tested decision — nothing to preview, so Done was "a target for nothing". That test is inverted: the reasoning holds just as well for the language grid, which is the one that prompted this. Closing that grid holds the dwells for a second by Cancel as well as by Done now, since either lands the pointer on a board that may have moved under it.

commits.subject: Make everything reachable by dwell, and every scroll scrollable by it (#75)

body.text: An audit of every control and every scrolling surface. Each gap below was something somebody working the board by gaze alone could see and could not use, and none of them failed a test — a test that clicks a control proves nothing about whether a rest on it does anything.

Fields that took the caret only on a click. The ElevenLabs key, the Anthropic key and the sync passphrase, a category's name, and the figures in a spinner. Peri's own keyboard types into whatever field has the caret, so the three account rows in Settings could not be set up by gaze at all. `DwellInput` was private to the Aliases panel; it is shared now and every single-line field is one. The figures are `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"`, because a number field refuses `setSelectionRange` and the first dwell to fire on one would have thrown.

Links that answered only to a press: the policy and terms from the sign-in page and the guide, and the way back from those pages. Somebody who reached the policy by dwell could read it and not leave it. `DwellLink` is a real anchor with the dwell hook's click in front of it, so a click in the second after the screen moved is refused there as it is everywhere else — on a gaze rig that sends real clicks, the click is the dwell. Same tab always: a new tab needs a press to be allowed.

Surfaces that scrolled by wheel alone. The slot chooser — fifty body parts on the chooser somebody opens to say which part of them hurts — and the legal pages, which now scroll in a `ScrollPane`. The edit strip scrolled sideways on a phone and no longer scrolls at all: the title gives way to an ellipsis and the category trigger never leaves it.

The two text boxes past their cap, which a textarea's lack of children left with nowhere to hang controls. `BoxScroll` puts an up and a down inside the box's right edge while there is more than shows, in padding the box gives up only then, inset from top and bottom by more than the strips on the border reach into it. `useScrollEdges` is the one answer to "is there more" for these and for `ScrollPane`.

The file button did nothing to a rest. A browser opens its picker only for a real press, so for a gaze user it is refused every time — which used to happen in silence. It asks through `showPicker`, the one of the two ways that says it was refused, and names Paste a backup when it is.

`tests/app/reach.test.tsx` drives each of these by resting and never by clicking. `tests/app/structure.test.ts` holds the source to it: an anchor only inside `DwellLink`, a field only inside `DwellInput`, no `<select>`, every textarea carrying the caret dwell, and every scrolling surface on a list naming what scrolls it — so the next one is a decision rather than a default.

commits.subject: Listen to a question, and offer a reply for it (#74)

items: Listen to a question, and offer a reply for it

body.text: Peri has always been one-directional. Somebody chooses phrases and the board says them; the person talking to them speaks into the room and leaves no trace of it anywhere. This writes that half down.

A microphone at the message box's upper-left corner opens a second text area above the message, holding what was just asked. The three corners of that border are now all spoken for, and each holds a different kind of thing: a mode in the middle, a value at the right, and at the left the one control that opens a surface of its own.

The heard box is a text box, so it answers to a dwell like the other one. A recogniser mis-hears names, and putting a caret in the middle of a sentence was the one thing a gaze user could never do about that. It fills as the words arrive, because a box that stays empty for four seconds and then fills is indistinguishable from a box that is broken.

Translating a heard question is the only place this app goes that direction, and it deliberately does not tell the service what language the question was in. What the setting holds is what the board is spoken as, and a nurse switching to English mid-sentence is the ordinary case. Naming it wrongly is worse than not naming it. The meaning goes under the words that were said, and a correction drops it.

The suggested reply is the riskiest thing in this app, and everything about it is arranged around one rule: a suggestion is never spoken. It lands in the message box, and it is said only when the person dwells on Speak, like any other message. The test asserts that with auto-speak on, which is the mode where everything else is spoken the moment it is chosen.

It never writes over words somebody already had. The composer's undo is a one-step toggle rather than a stack, so a suggestion replacing a half-written message could not be walked back past it — which would make accepting a machine's words a thing that happened to somebody rather than a thing they chose. The control goes quiet instead and says what would let it work.

The model is given a list of limits rather than an instruction to be clever: one short reply, first person, and nothing invented about a person it knows nothing about. A board answering "yes, I took them at eight" to a question about medication would be putting a clinical claim in somebody's mouth.

The key is the user's own. Not a preference: a Google key can be pinned to one site by referrer, which is what makes the translation key safe to inline, and nothing restricts an Anthropic key that way. So there is a Settings row beside ElevenLabs, following every rule that key follows.

Two disclosures, both in the Settings row, the guide and the privacy policy. The microphone's audio goes to the browser's own speech service. The question goes to Anthropic, on the user's own account, only when they ask for a reply.

items: Close the gaps mutation testing found in listen mode

body.text: One of them mattered more than the rest. Only the parts of a reply that are the reply were being taken, and nothing held it to that — a block of some other kind carrying a text field would have gone straight through. A model's own working, put into an assistive board's message box for somebody to say out loud, is the worst thing this feature could do.
Three more gaps, each a mutation that survived:
Nothing held the key to being in one place. It was asserted to be in the right header and not on the URL, which a copy into a second header passes.

Nothing held the microphone to closing with the screen. A microphone held open by a component nobody can see is the worst version of this, and nothing else in the app can turn it off once the screen that owns it is gone.
Nothing held the reply key to a storage name of its own. Every key here is a bare string under a bare name, so two sharing one would have each quietly overwriting the other.

Four guards turned out to be unreachable and are gone rather than kept. Two in the recogniser, where a browser with neither name and a browser that refuses to make one are the same failure through one catch, and where an empty tag is already what the API means by "the device decides". Two in the composer, where the history push claimed an undo it never gave — the control refuses to run over a message rather than offering to undo one.

One survivor stands and says so where it lives: dropping what was heard at the moment the box closes rather than when it is next opened changes nothing on screen and no test can see it. What differs is whether somebody's question is still held in memory after they have put it away.
Forty-six mutations, all forty-six killed.

items: Measure which microphone the recogniser is on, rather than believing it

body.text: Listen mode was asked for a setting to choose the microphone and its level. SpeechRecognition is documented to offer neither: no device option, no audio stream in, no gain. If that is right the setting cannot be built as asked, and a picker listing the inputs would move a control that steers nothing, which on a board aimed at by gaze is worse than no control at all.

So this measures it. The same answer the pointer probe gives about the pointer stream, for the same reason: an assumption about a browser API is worth less than one reading from the hardware in the room.

It opens every input at once with a live level meter, names which one the browser calls the system default, and logs each transcript beside whichever device was loudest when it arrived. Make one device hot and the rest cold, and that pairing says which device the recogniser was listening to. It also dumps every property a SpeechRecognition exposes and highlights anything naming a device, a stream or a gain, since a setting would have to hang on one of them.
Standalone HTML, no build step, and not in public/ for the reason the pointer probe is not: everything there ships to production and is indexed.

The structure test holds it to reaching for the same recogniser the app does, under both the prefixed and unprefixed names. An instrument measuring a different object from the one it is meant to be tuning answers a question nobody asked, which is the rule the pointer probe already lives under.

items: Let the model behind a suggested reply be chosen

body.text: It was pinned to Haiku 4.5 for latency, which is the right default and the wrong only option: a question that needs thinking about is worth waiting two seconds for, and that is a judgement only the person answering can make.

Three models, in the Suggested replies row and only once a key is set, since without one the choice would set nothing. They are ordered by how long they take, because that is the axis that matters here, and the quickest is the default for the reason the ElevenLabs voice is Flash.

A full screen of dwell tiles rather than a list that drops down, for the reason every choice in this app is one: an operating system draws a native list outside the page, where nothing can be hovered and so nothing can be dwelled.

A closed list rather than a free string, checked in three places — reading the stored settings, reading a backup, and once more in the service itself. A model name is handed to somebody else's API, so a board opened in a later release and then in this one would otherwise fail on the first question somebody was asked rather than in the settings panel. The third check is the one that matters, it being the last point before the name becomes a request.

items: Close the gaps mutation testing found in the model setting

body.text: Nothing held a backup to carrying a model that had actually been chosen. Only the nonsense case was covered, and that falls back to the default anyway, so a version that ignored the file entirely passed. The symptom would have been the setting quietly going back to Quickest every time a board was restored or arrived from another device.

And the service had a default of its own for the model as well as the check that falls back, which is two places saying the same thing. The check stays, since it is the last point before the name becomes somebody else's API call.
Sixteen mutations, all sixteen killed.

items: Let a suggested reply know the date, the world, and where to look things up

body.text: Three reasons it answered unlike the CLI does, and all three were mine.

It had no idea what day it is. A bare API call carries no clock, unlike the prompt behind an agent, so every question with a when in it was answered out of training data as though the year had not moved. Not refused, which would at least have read as a limit. The date is taken off the device now, since that is the clock the person being asked is living by.

The guard was written as facts in general. A model reads that as covering the capital of France, so it dodged questions nobody could come to harm over and the whole feature read as broken rather than careful. The line that matters is about whose facts: a board must never answer "yes, I took them at eight" to a question about medication. So the split is explicit now. The world it may answer for, the person it may not.

And it had no way to look anything up. Anthropic's own search tool, bounded to a single use, because this is the one capability here that costs seconds somebody is standing in front of them for. The model decides whether it needs one at all, so a question it already knows the answer to is as quick as it ever was.

A searched turn comes back as several blocks: what the model said before it looked anything up, the search, what came back, then the answer. Only the run of text after the last of those is the reply. Joining them all would put "let me look that up" into the message box in front of the words.
A search is a third disclosure, the question reaching a search provider as well as Anthropic, and it is in the Settings row, the guide and the privacy policy beside the other two.

items: Close the gaps mutation testing found in the searched reply

body.text: Two guards were doing one job. Everything after the last non-text block is text by construction, so the filter that then checked each block's type could never fire — it only made the cut look as though it were checked twice, and it hid the cut itself from being tested at all. With it gone, moving that cut by one block fails a test rather than passing quietly.
And nothing held a block whose words are not words. It would have been stringified into the message box, and `[object Object]` is a thing somebody would then be offered to say out loud.
Fifteen mutations, all fifteen killed.

items: Leave a gap to fill in, offer Fable, and keep the day's conversation

body.text: Three things, all about the reply being the person's rather than a machine's.

A gap, not a question back. What the model may not state about somebody it now leaves a hole in, and the hole is the app's own blank: the caret lands in it and the words are typed into the gap, exactly as a fill-in-the-blank phrase off the board works. Asking "which tablets?" was a machine interviewing somebody who is already having to spell their answers out one letter at a time.

Two or more underscores are taken as a gap, because a model asked for three will sometimes write two or four, and a reply with visible underscores in it is worse than a gap a character wider than it was asked for. A lone underscore is left alone, being a character somebody's name might have in it.

Fable 5.1 joins the list, last rather than slotted among the others: it is a different voice rather than a faster or a slower one, and the ordering claim the other three make is about how long they take.

And a day of questions and replies goes back with the next one, as the turns they were. Asked "tea or coffee" and then "milk?", a reply that had never seen the first would be answering a different question. Twenty exchanges at most, since every one is sent again and paid for in tokens and in the seconds somebody is waiting.

That record is what somebody was actually asked in a care room, so it follows the Sent list's rules exactly: its own key, never in a backup, never in a snapshot, cleared by a factory reset, and taken away with the key it belongs to. It is pruned on the way out as well as in, so a board left open overnight forgets on its own. There is a button in the Settings row for the person who wants it gone now rather than in the morning.

items: Cap the conversation on the way out as well as in

body.text: The limit was only applied as an exchange was added, so nothing held what came back from storage. What is there was not necessarily written by this release — a longer window from an earlier one, or a file somebody edited — and every turn read back is one more sent to the model and paid for in tokens and in seconds.
Twenty-three mutations, all twenty-three killed.

items: Put the question beside the answer where there is room for it

body.text: Listen mode stacked the heard box above the message, which pushes the grid down by the whole of that box and the row of tools under it. On a wide screen that is height the board cannot spare being spent where there is width nobody is using.

So at WIDE_ENOUGH the two share the line: 35% question, 65% message, 2rem between them. 2rem is this app's target-separation number rather than a spacing one — both boxes are dwell targets — so it is written as the flex gap, which does not shrink and is therefore a floor as well as a size. The heard box is capped there against the message box's own cap less its tools, so the two columns end on the same line and opening listen mode costs the board no height at all. It has to be capped by something: there are no dwell controls on that box, and whatever scrolls out of it is out of reach of the person reading it.

Neither strip on the border moves. Both hang off `.text-display-wrap`, which is the same size in the same place whether listen mode is open or not, so the microphone stays at one point on screen and merely rides a different box's corner. It is the way out of listen mode as well as the way in.

The wrapper was already a flex row, from when it held one box and two absolutely positioned strips — so the heard box had been sitting beside the message at whatever width a textarea's `cols` implies, rather than above it as everything describing it said. Both arrangements are deliberate now, and wrapping is what lets one rule lay out both.

How tall the message box may get becomes `--message-max-height`, because the heard box is capped against it and two numbers that have to add up are two numbers that come apart at the first change. The guard that read the cap out of the `.text-display` rule follows the token instead.
One breakpoint, not two: `topbar.tsx` asks the same question in JavaScript for the two pickers, which are not cheap to mount and hide, and `tests/app/structure.test.ts` holds the two together.

items: Move the slot that empties the box onto the box's left border

body.text: Clear and Undo — and in edit mode "start a new phrase" — were a full-size button in the rail beside the box. On the border they are the same bargain the mode strip already struck on the top one: the board gets 3.5rem of width back, and what it costs is a control painted small enough to sit on a border with an invisible area around it a head or eye tracker can still hit.

Two things about where it sits. It is measured 2.25rem down from the top of the box rather than centred on it, because the box grows downward to five lines and a centred control would slide down the border as somebody typed. And 2.25rem is the mode strip's own spacing rather than the 2rem `.topbar-choices` keeps between its two: the left border of a box 3.5rem tall is not long enough for two controls and 2rem of air, and three mode toggles already sit 2.25rem apart on this same bar. It is the most this border has to give.

These are the two controls on the box that paint nothing of their own, so each strip paints an opaque black ground — the reason `.topbar-modes` has one, and the reason `.topbar-choices` does not, its two painting `--bg` and drawing a border of their own.

`.keyboard-btn`'s margin widens to 1.75rem for the half of the new strip that hangs outside the border. At the 4px it was, that control's hit area reached a third of the way across the button beside it, which is two targets in one place. It costs 24px of the 64px that came back.

items: Move both strips onto the lower borders they belong to

body.text: Clear and Undo hung off `.text-display-wrap`, which holds both boxes — so on a wide screen with listen mode open it rode the *question's* left edge, and a Clear there is a Clear on somebody else's words. It hangs off `.message-wrap` now, a wrapper that exists only to be positioned against. The microphone and the two value controls stay on the pair: the wrapper is the same size in the same place whether listen mode is open or not, which is what holds them at one point on screen, and neither of them belongs to one box rather than the other.

It moves to the left end of the box's lower border, mirroring the microphone at the left end of the upper one. The upper border was full — a mode in the middle, the values at the right, the microphone at the left — and two controls on one side of a box 3.5rem tall cannot keep the air this app puts between gaze targets, while one at each end can, the distance only growing as the box does. Down there it shares the line with the edit strip, which is centred, and sits a layer above it: on a screen too narrow for that strip's content the two meet, and this is the smaller and the fixed one while the strip scrolls sideways to reach the rest of itself.

The heard box's three controls ride its lower border too, pulled up by half their own height and by the column gap they no longer sit below — both numbers named on `.heard-wrap` so the pull cannot come apart from what it is pulling. Each takes a black ground of its own, for the reason the mode strip is opaque: a control painted on a border with nothing behind it shows the border and the words through. A ground each rather than one pill, since two rem apart a pill would be wider than the pane the wide-screen split gives that box.

Stacked, the half that hangs down meets the mode strip standing up off the message box, so the row gap between the two boxes goes to 2rem. The stacked height is what it was before: the row those tools sat in was taller than the half of one that hangs into the gap now.

`.topbar` padding is equal top and bottom, half a strip's height either way, now that the box carries one on each border outside edit mode too. `.keyboard-btn`'s margin goes back to 4px, nothing hanging past the box's left edge any more.

items: Set the question in the same type as the answer

body.text: `.heard-text` was 1.05rem with no weight and no line height against the message box's 1.35rem at 500 and 1.4 — which made a hierarchy out of what is really two halves of one conversation, side by side on a wide screen and read at arm's length or more. The question is the half the person using the board did not write and has the most trouble following.

Two numbers follow from the type rather than from taste. The minimum height is one line of it plus this box's own padding, the way the message box's is derived. And the cap goes from six rem to eight and a half, which is the four lines it used to hold at the smaller size — a gaze user has no way to scroll this box, so what a cap cuts off is out of reach. The share of a short screen is deliberately not scaled with the type: that clause is about the board underneath rather than about how big the words are.
The padding stays tighter and the cap stays a line short of the message box's five. Those are about how much room the box takes, not about how the words in it are set.
Held by a test, because it is four declarations in two rules two hundred lines apart and a diff shows nothing.

items: Hold the two boxes to one height, and let both grow

body.text: The heard box never grew at all — it was a one-row textarea with a floor and a cap and `overflow-y: auto`, so a question longer than three lines scrolled, on a surface with no dwell control for scrolling and nothing to hang one on. What scrolled out of it was out of reach of the person reading it.

Both boxes are measured now, and both take the height of whichever is holding more. Side by side on a wide screen, two boxes of somebody's speech at different heights read as two unrelated things rather than as the two halves of one exchange; the question is not a caption on the answer. The measuring lives in `topbar.tsx` because the bar is the only thing that can see both, which is why the heard box's ref is made there and passed down rather than created in `HeardBox`.

Both are cleared before either is measured. `scrollHeight` includes whatever height a box is already holding, so one still standing at the other's would report it straight back and the pair would only ever grow.

Measurement only decides anything between the floor and the cap, so those have to match too or the pair comes apart while both are empty and again when either fills up. The heard box takes the message box's floor, cap and padding — the padding because two boxes of the same type at the same height that still started their first line a quarter of a rem apart would look like a mistake nobody could name. `--message-max-height` is `--box-max-height` now, being the cap on both.

Equal heights mean the pair can spend a third of a short screen each where before it was a third and a fifth, so stacked they are clamped to a fifth apiece — the share the question alone used to get. Written as a clamp on the shared cap rather than as a second value for it, and lifted on a wide screen where the two spend width instead. The selectors match only while the question is on screen: the heard box being in the document is the condition, so nothing has to say so in a class.

items: Answer a settled question without being asked, and say it is coming

body.text: Five things, and two of them were bugs.

**The heard box flickered under a resting pointer** because its dwell fill named `dwellFillH`, which animates the element's own `width` from nought. That is right for a `.dwell-bar` inside a control and, on a box with nothing inside it to be the bar, it is the box collapsing and growing back — text rewrapping and both boxes re-measuring all the way. The bar never showed either: `background-size` stayed at nought the whole time. It uses the painted fill the message box uses, renamed from `composerDwellFill` to `boxDwellFill` now that three boxes share it. That rename nearly took the Aliases panel's fields with it, so `tests/app/structure.test.ts` now holds every `animation` to keyframes that exist — a name nothing defines does not fail, it silently never runs.

**The message box had a double border** because `:focus-visible` draws a 3px ring two pixels outside it, and a focused box already says so by tinting its own border. Both boxes are out of that rule now, which is the same double line edit mode already avoids by tinting rather than outlining. The box carries `autoFocus`, so the app opened showing it.

The heard box loses its scrollbar, as the message box already had: the two are one box in two places, and a gutter that comes and goes on one of them changes the width the text wraps at, which changes the height, which is measured.

**A question that settles with nothing in the message box now answers itself.** The dwell it saves is the point — somebody has just been spoken to with a person waiting in front of them. On the recogniser stopping rather than on a final result: that is the one moment the whole of what was asked is in hand, and a reply to half a question is worse than none. Nothing is asked after a failure, nothing while there are words in the box, and nothing in edit mode, where the box is showing a phrase and a reply would land in the message behind it. `messageEmpty` goes into the hook and straight back out, so the control and the automatic asking cannot come to disagree.

**And the box the reply is coming to says so**, standing where the first line of it will be, in the placeholder's grey and the box's own type. It is the one thing here that waits somewhere other than the corner, because those seconds are now seconds in which nothing has happened as far as the person can tell. `Heard.working` becomes `asking`, since only one of the two lands in that box.
`useSettled` moves to `ui/settle.ts`: two things reach for it now, and a hook exported from `controls.tsx` costs fast refresh to nearly every screen here.

items: Give every border one kind of thing, and empty the rail

body.text: The heard box gets the message box's own two glyphs for emptying itself, first in its row of tools. One box is what somebody is being asked and the other is what they are about to say, and a control meaning "empty this" has to look the same on both or it is two controls to learn. It is also the gesture most worth being able to take back here: a recogniser mis-hears, the answer to a question that came out as nonsense is to empty the box, and what that throws away is the only copy of what was said to somebody. A one-step toggle like the composer's. Listening again clears the stack — that is a box filling with something new rather than one emptied on purpose, and an undo reaching past it would put back words nobody is talking about any more. The meaning does not come back with the words, for the reason a correction drops it.

The three that act on the message — speak, copy, paste, and in edit mode save, delete, paste — move to the right end of the box's upper border, where the language and the voice used to sit. Those go to the right end of the lower one: neither is about the message and neither is urgent, they are set once and left, which is the border to be on.
That empties the rail. What is left beside the box is the menu and the keyboard, which are about the app rather than about the message, and the board gets the whole of the width that came back.

`.topbar-actions` packs its three 1.25rem apart rather than the mode strip's 0.75rem. That much clears the invisible area each carries, so no two of them overlap anywhere. The modes can afford to be tighter: they are three states of one thing and picking the wrong one costs a dwell to put back, while one of these deletes a phrase.

Both strips hang off `.message-wrap` rather than the pair of boxes, the rule the slot that empties the box already follows: they act on the message, and with listen mode open on a wide screen the pair's corners belong to the question.

So each border now holds one kind of thing. Upper: a mode in the middle, the microphone at the left, the actions at the right. Lower: the slot that empties the box at the left, the edit strip in the middle, the two values at the right.

items: Show the icons the guide names, and say the bar is blue

body.text: The guide named buttons in words — "the speaker button", "the pencil", "the tick" — for controls that are a glyph and nothing else, because there is no room on a border for a word. That asks somebody to match a description against a picture, which is what this app's readers are least able to do quickly. A line of prose can name an icon now and it is drawn where it stands.

The mark is `:speak:`. Braces were the obvious shape and are the one this text cannot use: the guide teaches `{pronouns}` and `{'red', 'blue'}` as the syntax for a phrase's own choices, so a brace-delimited mark would have eaten the very words explaining it. A name nothing defines draws nothing, silently, so `tests/app/structure.test.ts` holds every name the guide and the legal pages use to the table.

The emergency bar has been blue since the reorder work and the guide, the comments and AGENTS.md all still called it red. Red in this app means destruction — delete a phrase, empty the board, sign out — and a red bar along the bottom said "careful" where it needed to say "here, now".
Several passages became lists: what rides which edge of the message box, what the three modes are, what changes in edit mode, what the buttons above an alias list do.
The rest is the app catching up with itself.

Speak is a 3rem glyph at the end of its row, against the 1.5rem of the two beside it. Everything else on that border edits what is in the box and this is what takes it out of the box and into the room, so it is the one thing there worth aiming at without looking. Save takes the same place at the same size in edit mode, and paste keeps the middle, being the one of the three that means the same either way.

The phrase voice picker leaves the edit strip: in edit mode the two controls at the box's lower-right corner are the phrase's own — the voice it is said in, and the language that voice is for. One pair of controls meaning whichever of the two the mode says, rather than two pairs that look alike and are not. That pair is drawn at any width in edit mode, unlike outside it: it is the only place a phrase can be given a voice now, and a control that exists on a monitor and not on a phone is a feature somebody cannot reach.

And the heard box loses its microphone button. Clearing it starts listening and undo stops it, because emptying that box has one reason behind it — what came back was wrong — and what somebody wants next is to be listened to again. A row with a listen button in it asked for two dwells out of one intention.

commits.subject: Close the gaps mutation testing found in the Translations tab

body.text: Four of the seven survivors were real. Every one of them was about the same thing: with no translation key in a test, a phrase that is wrongly put through the translator comes back as the words it went in as, so the whole point of not translating twice was invisible.

The traps that make it visible are a seeded table that would translate the French too, and a board set back to English while the tab still holds Spanish. Looked up a second time the cell comes out as something else entirely, and spoken off the board's language rather than its own it comes out in the wrong voice. `speak` now has its own tests for both halves of the contract the tab rests on: which paths report a translation, which of the three fallbacks report nothing, and that words already translated are said as they stand, as their own language, and never sent anywhere.
Nothing held the class that makes a two-line cell stack. jsdom lays out no differently either way, so the assertion is that the class is applied.

Two survivors were equivalent, and one of them was a guard doing a job something else already does: `speak` reports only the paths that translate, and the already-translated path returns before every one of them, so the caller needed no second guard. Removed rather than kept, since dead code that looks load-bearing is worse than none.
Thirty-nine mutations, all thirty-nine killed.

commits.subject: Keep what was said in another language, under a tab of its own

body.text: The board stays in the user's own words and the translation is what comes out, so until now a translation lasted exactly as long as it took to speak. There was nowhere to see what had been said and no way to say it again without going back through the service and paying for it twice.

There is a Translations tab now, pinned at the very end of the category bar and always newest first. A cell draws what came out of the speaker with the board's own wording under it, because without the second line the tab is a wall of text the person using the board cannot read.

It is not a category, and the two properties asked for are why. Its filter id begins with a space, exactly as Sent's does, which is what lets it be pinned where a custom order cannot reach it and ordered where the control cannot change it. A real category would be renameable, movable, deletable, and in every backup.

An entry belongs to a language as well as to a phrase, so the same words said in Spanish and in French are two entries and said twice in Spanish are one. The tag is what is stored rather than the table, because es-PR reads the es-419 table and is spoken as es-PR, and a table could not say which voice to use or what to call it.

Saying one again does not translate it again. Without that the service would be asked for Spanish from Spanish, and the Spanish would be filed as a translation of itself, so the tab would grow every time it was used. It is said in the voice remembered for its language, which is what voicesByLanguage has always been for.

speak now reports what came out, on the two paths that translate and on none of the three that fall back to the words as written: a phrase spoken as it was written is not a translation, and an entry claiming otherwise would be wrong in a list somebody reads. A callback rather than a write from inside speak, because the caller decides whether it counts. The emergency bar does not, for the reason it counts no usage either: that surface exists to not wait on anything, and a storage write on the way to saying "Help me!" is what it must not pick up.

It never leaves the device. Its own key, out of every backup and every snapshot, cleared by a factory reset, for the reason the Sent list and the usage record are not in one: it is what somebody actually said.

commits.subject: Close the gaps mutation testing found in the clip store

body.text: One of them was a real bug. `drop` answers with a value rather than throwing, so a refused DELETE was walked straight past and the list of clips was taken away over the top of it — leaving somebody's words at an address nothing now named, after they had asked for them back. The list goes only if every clip went, which is the other half of writing it first, and a second run finishes the job.
Four gaps in the tests, each a mutation that survived:

Nothing held a clip read off the disk to being kept in memory. The emergency bar asks a synchronous lookup that sees only memory, so a phrase given its own voice is in memory after a reload or it is not in the right voice at all.

Nothing held a clip's address apart from the board's. Every address comes out of the same expansion, so the only thing keeping a clip from landing on top of the board is the string each is derived under. Asked now of the awkward keys as well as a real one, including the one that is the whole reason a clip's prefix ends in a colon.
Nothing read back a clip whose bytes are not text, which would hand a speaker a blob of junk rather than buying the clip again.
Nothing ran the clean-up against a list it could not entirely trust.

Twenty-eight mutations, twenty-seven killed. The survivor is equivalent and says so where it lives: only this user's own devices can write that blob, so the type guard cannot change what happens today, and it is there to make the declared type true for the two callers that read it.

commits.subject: Stop buying the same ElevenLabs clip twice

body.text: A clip is billed per character and is decided entirely by the voice and the words, so the same phrase is the same bytes for ever and on every device. Four places are now asked before ElevenLabs is, in the order they cost least.

The stored layer was the bug. Every clip fetched has always been written to IndexedDB and nothing ever read one back except the handful of phrases carrying their own voice — so a reload bought the whole board again, one phrase at a time, with the audio already sitting on disk unread. It is read on the way to the network now rather than all at once on arrival, which is work nobody asked for; the clips that must be in hand before they are wanted are still warmed by name.

The remote layer is new. With Synchronize on, a clip one device paid for is found by the others. Each clip is its own blob and never part of the board: audio is bought by speaking rather than by editing, and folding it in would make saying a phrase look like an edit and push a board nobody changed. A clip's address is derived from the words and the voice through the same HKDF the board's address comes out of, so a second device works out where a clip is from the phrase already on its board and there is nothing to look up. The server is handed a different 256-bit number for every clip and can tell nothing from any of them.

One list is kept beside the clips, and it exists for exactly one reason. Stop and erase the copy has to take the audio too, and an address nobody wrote down is an address nobody can delete. So the list is written before the clip it names and the invariant runs one way only: it may name a clip that is not there, which costs a wasted DELETE, while a clip the list does not name would be somebody's words left on a server after they asked for them back.

Two costs, both deliberate. A genuine miss now waits on one more request, and never on the emergency bar, which returns before any of this is reached. The list is rewritten whole each time it grows, which is bandwidth rather than time because sending it is never waited on.
voice/ and sync/ are the same line of the layering, so neither imports the other: the cache takes a remote layer that talk.tsx installs, being the only thing that can see both.
The three documents that have to agree about what leaves the device all say that the audio travels and that erasing the copy takes it.

commits.subject: Start every tab on Most used, and stop offering All an order it cannot hold

body.text: A board arrives with two and a half thousand phrases in whatever order the table happens to list them, and the phrase somebody wants next is nearly always one they have wanted before. So Most used is where every tab now starts. Nothing is lost by that: a phrase nobody has used keeps the place the board gave it, so a board that has not been talked with yet looks exactly as it always did and sorts itself out as it is spoken.
The consequence is that the board rearranges live by default, which is only safe because of the guard that already holds every dwell until the pointer is aimed somewhere else.

All offers no Custom order. A hand arrangement belongs to one category and All shows every category at once, so there is nothing there for it to be an arrangement of. Hiding a tile that is also a tab's way home is how you strand somebody, so `sortFor` reads a stored `custom` under All as the default — and it is why the default had to move off `custom` at the same time. One flag, `canArrange`, answers both halves: whether a tab offers the tile, and whether its phrases can be arranged by hand. It is false for All and for Sent.
Sent and the emergency bar are untouched. Sent keeps its own newest-first order and its control stays switched off; the red bar has its own hand arrangement and never reaches any of this.

Two things in the tests had to move with it. A tap is answered exactly as a dwell is, so a click that fires with no pointer movement is now refused after the board rearranges — the app tests click through a pointer that travelled, as the sorting tests already did. And the two loops that filled a slot picker are bounded, because the one that was not turned that refusal into a suite that hung silently rather than a test that failed.

commits.subject: Give a tap the same answer a dwell gets

body.text: Both guards gated only the hover-and-hold path, so a real click walked straight past them. That matters more than it looks: a gaze rig can be set to send a left click where it rests, and on the device this app is for the click *is* the dwell — the operating system is doing the holding. A guard the platform walks around is not a guard, and the symptom is the one the whole scheme exists to prevent: a phrase spoken that nobody chose.

It cost a session's debugging to learn. A report of the board selecting the cell under the pointer after a live re-sort looked exactly like the new guard failing, and I diagnosed a browser hit-testing race that was not there.

`screenJustMoved` is the single question both routes now ask. **Enter and Space are deliberately left alone**: they are aimed by focus rather than by position, and focus follows its element when the screen moves, so there is nothing for the pointer's stillness to say about them — and guarding them would leave a keyboard user with no working control.
What it costs is a mouse user losing a click in the second after a panel closes, the text size changes, or the order picker closes. That is the same second their hover dwell was already deaf for.

Fourteen tests failed on the change and every one was the guard working. Thirteen were clicking twice where a real pointer would have travelled in between, so the sorting suite's click helper moves the pointer first — which is what a click is. The fourteenth closed a panel and clicked inside the same second, which is precisely the case `holdDwells` was written for.

commits.subject: Keep the last phrase said marked until anything else fires

body.text: It was a third of a second of tint on a timer, which stopped working once the board could rearrange itself on the dwell that rearranged it: a flash on a cell that is moving at the same moment. A mark that lasts is what says *that one, and it went there*.

It ends on the next dwell rather than on a clock — any dwell, not only another phrase. What it claims, that this is the last thing you did, stops being true the moment anything else happens, and a timer would take it away while somebody was still reading the board for it.

`onDwellActivation` is the mechanism: one listener set in the dwell module, told **before** each control's own action. That ordering is the whole of why a phrase cell can clear the old mark and set its own in one breath rather than clearing the one it has just set.

The cell takes a boolean rather than the id, so the memo holds for every cell but the two that change, and `aria-current` says by ear what the tint says by eye. Edit mode and arranging mark nothing: neither reaches the selection path, and a cell there is a phrase being opened or lifted.

Two gaps came out of mutating it. Nothing tested that unsubscribing stops a listener, which would have leaked a setState on an unmounted grid for every dwell in the app, and nothing tested the before-not-after ordering.

commits.subject: Remember each tab's own order, and bring it back when the tab opens

body.text: The chosen order is kept per tab now, keyed by the tab's filter id — a category's name, or `all` — rather than one order for the whole board.

The categories are not alike. A long reference list is worth having alphabetically, a short one worth having by what gets used, and a category somebody arranged by hand worth leaving as they arranged it, so a single setting makes each of those the wrong answer everywhere else. This reverses the reasoning the last commit wrote down, which was that a button meaning something different under every tab is one nobody could learn. The answer to that was already in the control: it says which order is on, in its glyph and in its name, so a tab sorted differently reads rather than mystifies.

A tab nobody has chosen for shows the board's own order, and choosing that order drops the entry rather than storing it — a record that is all defaults is an empty one, the rule the phrase arrangements follow. A single order written by the previous version lands on All rather than being thrown away: it was chosen while looking at some tab, and All is the one the board opens on.

Two test gaps of the same shape came out of mutating this, and an array is both: it is the damage that survives a parse, because its indices become keys. A stored `["alpha"]` read back as an order remembered for a tab called "0", and a stored array of usage entries as counts for phrases called "0" and "1". The second was there before this change.

commits.subject: Close three gaps mutation testing found in the arranging tests

body.text: A backup carrying nothing but an arrangement counted as empty, and the test that was meant to catch it could not: a whole-app backup always carries the settings, so `empty` was false whatever the arrangement counted for. It is scoped now, where neither the settings nor the word lists ride along, and it asserts that the same file without the arrangement really is empty.
A deleted phrase stayed in the arrangement, and an emptied arrangement kept its category's key. Neither had a test at all.

The held phrase was not put down when the mode was switched off. Without the release, lifting one, toggling the mode off and on, then dwelling another drops the forgotten one instead of lifting the cell under the pointer.

commits.subject: Let a category be arranged by hand, in edit mode

body.text: The fourth surface that can be arranged, out of the same `ui/reorder` as the category tabs and the emergency bar: one dwell picks a phrase up, a second on another drops it there, and a mouse can drag instead. Edit mode only, and its own mode within it — a third flag beside the other two, because arming the board somebody speaks with while they tidy their tabs is what separate flags exist to prevent.

`PhraseStore.phraseOrder` is per category, keyed by the category's shown name and valued by phrase ids. That is the unit somebody actually arranges, and one flat list would have to name every phrase in the table the first time anything moved. It is also why All cannot be arranged: its phrases come from every category at once, and ranking them against each other's arrangements would interleave orders that were never about one another. The control goes quiet there and on Sent rather than going away, and says why.

A move captures the order that was on screen and switches the grid to Custom order, the rule the category tabs follow and for the same reason — a move applied to a hidden order lands somewhere nobody could see, and an arrangement nobody is looking at is not an arrangement. So sorting A to Z and moving a few is a way to build one.
`orderEmergency` is `orderByIds` now: the bar is one category's worth of buttons and a category is one tab's worth of cells, and the arithmetic never cared which.

It travels in a backup, trimmed to the categories in scope — unlike the bar's, which is one category's and goes whole or not at all — and merges behind what the receiving device had already arranged. A rename carries the arrangement to the new name, and a rename that collapses two categories appends the incoming one behind the one it joins.

commits.subject: Rearrange the board as it is used, and hold the dwell until the gaze moves

body.text: The orders that follow use now follow it on the dwell that used the phrase, rather than settling until the tab or the order changed.

What that costs is the thing this app has to be careful about: the pointer is somebody's gaze and it rests where it last fired, so the cell that lands underneath after the rearrangement gets a `pointerenter` of its own, which is an instruction nobody gave. `holdDwellsUntilMoved` is the answer, beside the timed guard rather than instead of it — a second of deafness is both too long for somebody who has already looked away and too short for a gaze that stays put. Arming only ever happens on arrival, so this is exactly "nothing may be chosen until the pointer leaves the thing it is on": the cell that arrives is refused and stays refused until the pointer leaves it and enters something else. It clears on movement, which is the same rule from the other side — a pointer cannot leave what it is on without moving — and that is also the half that covers nothing landing under the pointer at all.

The live order forced out a real bug. The grid restarted its render window whenever the phrase array changed identity, which is now every utterance: the grid would have shrunk back to one screenful mid-conversation and taken the view with it. The window keys on what makes it a different list — the tab and the word being typed — rather than on the array.

commits.subject: Say what the usage record is, and keep the grid's memo holding

body.text: Three things the first commit left:

`handleSelectPhrase` reaches every one of a couple of thousand memoised cells, and it depended on the whole `useUsage` result — a fresh object every render, so the memo would never have held. It takes the two functions now, the shape `deliverPhrase` already uses.

The privacy policy lists what the app keeps on the device and claims to be everything it remembers, so how often each phrase is used is on that list, with a line saying it is the one item there that goes nowhere at all: not in a backup file, and not in what Synchronize sends.

AGENTS.md gains an "Ordering the grid" section for the parts a diff cannot show — why the order settles rather than following every dwell, why arranging happens before the search ranks anything, and why the board's own order is the same array rather than a copy of it.

commits.subject: Let the grid be ordered by use, by name, or as it is

body.text: Four arrangements, offered under every category tab from one button at the top of the grid rail: the board's own order, A to Z, what was used most recently, and what is used most often. A full-screen picker rather than a cycling glyph — four states behind one mark is three dwells and a guess.

**A usage order settles rather than following every dwell.** Using a phrase counts it immediately; the board only rearranges when the tab or the order changes. Live re-sorting is the obvious reading and the wrong behaviour here: the pointer is somebody's gaze and it rests where it last fired, so a board that reordered itself the instant a phrase was spoken would slide a different phrase under that gaze and say that one too — and take the view back to the top mid-conversation.
Arranging happens before the search ranks anything, so a typed word still puts the best match first and the chosen order decides the ties behind it.

How much each phrase is used is kept under its own key and is never in a backup or a snapshot, for the reason the Sent list is not: it is a record of what somebody actually said and how often, and a backup is a file made to be handed to somebody else. Sent keeps its own order and the control goes quiet rather than away while it is showing.

commits.subject: Bump vitest from 4.1.10 to 4.1.11

body.text: Bumps [vitest](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/tree/HEAD/packages/vitest) from 4.1.10 to 4.1.11. - [Release notes](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/releases) - [Changelog](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/blob/main/docs/releases.md) - [Commits](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/commits/v4.1.11/packages/vitest)
--- updated-dependencies: - dependency-name: vitest dependency-version: 4.1.11 dependency-type: direct:development ...

commits.subject: Set the two corner buttons two rem apart

body.text: Not spacing — target separation. These are aimed at by gaze, and two controls close enough for the jitter to cross between them is one control that does the wrong thing. Two rem also clears the invisible hit area each one carries: `.choice-btn::before` reaches 6px past every edge, so anything under 12px would have them overlapping where nothing is drawn.

The strip's own black pill goes with it. It was there for the mode strip's reason — that one is opaque because its three controls are transparent and the message box shows through between them — but each of these paints `--bg` and draws a border of its own, so all the pill added at this distance was a black band across the gap.

commits.subject: Remember a voice for each language, and for each phrase in each

body.text: A voice is a language, so switching the board between two of them used to let go of the old voice and leave the browser to pick. That made choosing one a thing to redo rather than a thing to set — twice a day for anybody working in two languages, and every time for a phrase given a voice of its own, which came back read by a synthesiser for the wrong language.
Both halves are kept now. `settings.voicesByLanguage` is the board's, and `PhraseStore.voiceOverrides` becomes id → language → voice. Five things follow, and each has a test:

items: **The lookup is exact and never falls back to another language.** A phrase given an English voice has not been given a Spanish one, and an English synthesiser reading Spanish is worse than the board's own voice, which is what nothing means.

**`''` is a key like any other**, the board following the device being a setting somebody chose a voice under too. It is where a store or a backup written before this reads its single voice, that being very nearly always the language it was picked in.

**`chooseLanguage` writes down the voice it is leaving.** A device restored from an older backup has a `voiceURI` and an empty map, and without that the first switch away throws the voice away — the exact loss this exists to stop.

**`setVoiceOverride` is in core rather than in `useBoard`.** The rule it exists for is that giving a phrase a voice in one language keeps every other language's, and while the arithmetic sat in a hook that mutation survived: nothing could reach it without driving the whole app through two language changes to watch one object.
**The backup carries `voices` and still reads `voice`.** The writer emitted the map and both parsers dropped it, which cost nothing on the way out and lost every per-phrase voice on the way back in.

body.text: The pair are also at the message box's upper-right corner on a wide screen, riding the same border the modes ride at its middle, with the values on their faces — `en-US`, `Samantha` — in six rem and an ellipsis past that. `.text-display-wrap` exists only so that strip can hang off the box: everything else here centres on the bar, which is 4px off the box's centre and invisible, but a corner found that way would be out by the width of the action rail. It is never the mode strip, which holds exactly three found by position without being read.

commits.subject: Bring the keyboard forward onto today's main

body.text: Rebase repairs, and nothing else. The branch was cut before the tree was formatted, so every conflict was the formatter's wrapping rather than any real overlap — and three of them I made worse resolving: a union merge ate the opening of a doc comment in App.test.tsx, duplicated the React import in talk.tsx, and kept the pre-QWERTY wording of the `core/keys.ts` line in AGENTS.md when the second commit had already rewritten it.
Typecheck, lint and 1068 tests pass — the 1014 on main and 54 here.

commits.subject: QWERTY, and short enough to leave a board

body.text: Three changes to the keyboard.

QWERTY, which is a concession rather than a design: the frequency layout really is less travel, and travel is what a gaze pointer pays for, but nobody has ever seen one and every letter has to be hunted for until it is learnt.

Height cut from 46dvh to 30dvh, with tighter gutters. Typing narrows the board to what matches, so the point of typing is to reach a phrase in three letters rather than write it out -- and a keyboard that leaves no board leaves nothing to narrow.
That narrowing already worked; it is now held by tests through the keys themselves, in all three modes.

commits.subject: Draw the keyboard, because iOS will not

body.text: On iOS a pointer that only hovers cannot type anywhere in the app. The software keyboard is raised by a gesture and its keys are pressed by taps, and a dwell is a timer firing with neither. So Peri draws its own out of the same dwell controls as everything else.

It types into whatever field has the caret rather than into any box it knows about, which is what lets one keyboard serve the message box, the Aliases panel, a category name, the passphrase and the API key.
The letters are frequency-ordered, commonest nearest the middle: a gaze pointer pays for distance in a way a finger does not. The digits are not -- a number is read as a sequence.

commits.subject: Translate the shipped table into Spanish, French and Vietnamese

body.text: Machine output from `pnpm translate`, which is what that tool is for: the phrases Peri comes with are translated ahead of the build so the board speaks instantly, offline, and above all so the emergency bar never waits on a network.
Four tables, ~2,100 phrases each: es, es-419 (read by es-PR), fr, vi.

**This is not reviewed.** These are phrases somebody will say to a nurse about their own body, and a plausible-looking mistranslation is worse than an English sentence a listener has to work at. The six the red bar speaks are hand-written and correct in all four; everything else is Google's, and wants a speaker of each language reading it before anyone relies on it. Committed because a file in the tree can be corrected in place, which nothing in a terminal can.

commits.subject: Hold every table to the six phrases the red bar speaks

body.text: Vietnamese arrived with 2,106 phrases and no emergency bar. The tool generates from the phrase table, those six are not in it, and it *merges* — which protects them where a file already exists and gives a brand-new language none at all. Nothing threw, and no test failed, because the test named `['es', 'fr']`. A board set to Vietnamese would have answered its red bar in English.
So the test reads the directory now, and a language added tomorrow cannot skip the check. Two things it needs to be worth anything:

items: `tagFor`, because a table is named for the variety rather than the tag. `es-419.json` is reached by asking for `es-PR`; passing the file name through would test `es` twice and `es-419` never.
A guard that there are tables at all, or `it.each` passes by having nothing to iterate.

body.text: The six Vietnamese phrases are hand-written, placed first so the next run of the tool merges around them rather than through them. **They want a Vietnamese speaker's eye**: `Cứu tôi với!` is the emergency "save me" rather than the general "help me", which is the right register for a bar somebody reaches for without reading it, but that is a judgement this repo cannot make for itself. 911 is left as 911 — changing it to 115 is a decision about where somebody is, not a translation.

commits.subject: Install the tool pnpm translate has always named

body.text: `translate` runs `tsx`, and tsx was never a dependency — so the script that builds the shipped translation tables had never once run. It is the second broken script found today: `format` named an oxfmt that turned ninety files into invalid syntax. Neither was visible in a diff, and neither was reachable from a test.

Adding tsx surfaced something worse. It pulls in esbuild's install script, and pnpm will not run one without permission — a refusal that fails *every* pnpm command with ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS, `pnpm check` and the Netlify build included. The prompt was already waiting unanswered in two places: the global pnpm config, and a pnpm-workspace.yaml that was untracked, so git had never seen it and CI never would.

pnpm 11 no longer reads the `pnpm` field in package.json — neither onlyBuiltDependencies nor allowBuilds does anything there — so the answer goes in pnpm-workspace.yaml, which is committed. Left untracked, pnpm writes the placeholder again on the next machine and the deploy stops.
The answer is yes, and it is not a new trust decision: esbuild is how Vite builds this app and runs on every build whatever that file says.
structure.test.ts now holds every script to a command this project installs. It does not run them — `dev` never exits and `translate` would spend money — it checks the claim underneath both failures.

commits.subject: Make pnpm check refuse an unformatted tree

body.text: The reason the tree was unformatted for its whole life is that nothing ever asked. Fixing the formatter without this leaves the same hole: the next person to run `pnpm format` gets another sixty-file diff, and the one after that finds it corrupting things again if the version ever slips back.

`format:check` goes first because it is the cheapest thing in the chain — about 20ms against ninety files. An unformatted tree now fails in under a second and names the file, rather than after three minutes of tests.
It delegates to the `format` script rather than restating its paths, so the two cannot come apart about which directories are formatted.

**This makes formatting a deploy gate**, since `pnpm check` is the Netlify build command. That is the point, but the failure reads as a mysterious red build to whoever meets it first, so netlify.toml says beside the command that the fix can be `pnpm format`.

commits.subject: Format the tree

body.text: Mechanical, and separated from the commit that fixed the formatter so that one stays readable. Nothing here is a decision: it is what `pnpm format` now produces, mostly normalising prose that was wrapped in one file and not in the next.
Typecheck, lint and 1009 tests pass, and a second run of the formatter reports no differences.

commits.subject: Make pnpm format safe to run

body.text: Running the documented format command corrupted the tree. oxfmt 0.2.0 drops the `;` separators inside TypeScript type literals — `{ id: string; label: string }` became `{ id: string label: string }`, which is not valid syntax, in about ninety files at once. Nothing caught it, because pnpm check does not run the formatter.
Three things were wrong, and the version was only the first:

items: **0.2.0.** The `^0.2.0` caret pins to the 0.2.x line, so it never moved; latest is 0.65. The type-literal bug is gone there.

**No config, so the defaults fight this codebase.** oxfmt would put a semicolon on every statement, double-quote every string and wrap every sole arrow parameter in parentheses. Not corruption, but still a rewrite of the whole tree. printWidth is 115 because that is the width measured to disturb the fewest files, not because it is a round number.

**oxfmt formats JSON, CSS, HTML and YAML too.** Left to itself it reflows the 44,000-line phrase table, index.css — whose order is load-bearing and only checkable against a deploy preview — the pointer probe, and the lockfile. Scoped twice, in ignorePatterns and in the script's own arguments, so the two would have to fail together.

body.text: The tree is formatted in the commit after this one, which is mechanical and separable. From here the formatter is idempotent: a second run reports no differences.

commits.subject: Carry the translation key, rather than asking for one

body.text: Setting a spoken language used to mean opening a Google Cloud account first. That is not a setting, it is a wall — and the people this feature is for are the least able to climb it.

So Peri carries its own key: VITE_GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_KEY, out of .env.local in development and the site's environment on a deploy, inlined by Vite. The Translation row is gone, and with it checkKey, loadTranslateKey, saveTranslateKey and the peri_translate storage key. No device holds a translation key now, which answers three questions at once that each needed answering separately before: it is not in a backup, not in a sync snapshot, and not in the reset list. The ElevenLabs key stays the user's, because that one bills them for a voice they chose.

A key in a public bundle is safe by restriction, not by secrecy: HTTP referrer to this site, API restriction to Cloud Translation alone. What a lifted key then costs is quota rather than anybody's words.
Three things fall out of it:

items: hasTranslateKey() is asked before the async path starts rather than left to the client to refuse. With no key the words have to go out in the same tick; a promise resolving into the original a moment later is a phrase that arrives after it was needed.
GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_KEY and VITE_GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_KEY are different keys. A referrer is exactly what Node does not send, so pnpm translate takes an unrestricted one off the command line.

Tests run with no key unless one is stubbed in. Vitest loads .env.local, so without clearing it a machine with a real key runs different tests from CI — and the ones that matter most here are about there being no key at all.

body.text: The disclosure moves onto the Spoken language row, since that is now the control that starts phrases leaving the device, and SettingRow grows an optional note to carry it. It is a broadening, and the privacy policy says so: phrases are sent whenever a language is set, on our account rather than the user's. The guide and the policy are updated to match — the same three-documents rule the ElevenLabs disclosure follows.

commits.subject: Warn in the console when a service fails

body.text: Every service call here is written so that failing changes as little as possible -- sync fails into a line of text, a translation into the words as written, an ElevenLabs voice into the device's. That is right, and it is what makes the failures invisible: a board that carries on working looks like a board with nothing wrong.
reportFailure gives them one shape: [Peri] sync/pull: Server said 500.

Never the words and never the key -- a console ends up in every screen-share from then on. And only actual faults: a 409 is somebody writing first, a damaged backup is a defined path, and warning about those would fill the console during normal use.

commits.subject: Google Translate instead of DeepL

body.text: One API key rather than two hosts, and far more languages. It does not gain Patois: the 110-language expansion in 2024 went to Google Translate the product, not to Cloud Translation, which a page can call. Patois stays shipped-table-only either way.
