Puerto Rican Spanish asks for plain es -- Google's es-419 is on the LLM model, which wants a service account. The regional wording lives in the shipped table instead, which is now named for the variety rather than a provider's code, the provider having changed once already.
Google escapes its answer even when plain text is asked for. Unescaped, a synthesiser reads I'm cold as I ampersand hash thirty-nine m cold -- so it is decoded, by hand rather than through innerHTML.

commits.subject: Puerto Rican Spanish, and Jamaican Patois

body.text: A tag is not enough once regions are involved: what to say it as, what to translate it with, and which shipped table it reads are three questions, and for these they have three answers.
Puerto Rican Spanish goes to DeepL's ES-419. Nobody has a Puerto Rican target, and European Spanish would give a board vosotros and coger -- the second of which means something else in San Juan.

Patois is a language, not an accent, and no service translates into it. So it is the case the shipped tables exist for: the phrases Peri ships are written out ahead of time, and anything else is spoken as it was written, because there is nowhere to send it. It is spoken as en-JM, there being no Patois voice anywhere.
The language picker now offers what the device can speak OR Peri can translate into. The old rule blocked exactly these two.

commits.subject: Translate a phrase, and say it in a voice for the language

body.text: The board stays as it was written -- somebody goes on reading their own phrases in their own words -- and what comes out of the speaker is translated, for a listener who does not share their language.

Two sources. The phrases Peri ships are translated ahead of time, committed, and lazily loaded: instant, offline, free, and already in hand when the emergency bar is pressed. Everything else -- a phrase somebody wrote, one with a blank filled in, a message built out of several -- goes to DeepL once and is kept.
Never silence. A phrase that cannot be translated is said as it was written: a listener who has to work at it is recoverable, and nothing said at all is not.

commits.subject: A language to speak the board in

body.text: settings.language, a BCP-47 tag, with a picker of the languages this device actually has voices for -- offering one it cannot speak would be offering silence.

A chosen voice still wins, because choosing one is the more specific thing to have done. What the setting is for is the case where the voice does not apply: a voiceURI is a platform string and it travels between devices, so a board set up on a Mac arrives on a phone naming a voice that does not exist there. Without a language that falls back to whatever the system speaks, which is how an English board ends up read aloud in another language.
Changing the language lets go of a device voice that does not match it. An ElevenLabs voice is left alone -- it has no language of its own.

commits.subject: Keep the pointer probe as a tool

body.text: It found the failure; it is also what STALL_MS gets tuned with, so it now measures the stream as well as logging events: cadence, largest gap, drift per move, and whether the streaming signature currently holds. The block-the-main- thread buttons cover the one thing that could make a present pointer look absent.
Not in public/ -- everything there ships to production and is indexed. It restates the constants from ui/dwell.ts, and structure.test.ts fails if the two ever disagree.

commits.subject: Say when the app is waiting

body.text: Two things can keep somebody waiting: an exchange with the sync server, and re-parsing the phrase table after an alias list changes. Neither said anything before.

It waits 250ms before appearing. Both are usually over in a few milliseconds, and a spinner that shows for fifty of them is a flicker -- which costs more here than elsewhere, because the pointer is the user's gaze: something that catches the eye does not merely distract, it aims.

commits.subject: Hold back a dwell when the pointer stops sending

body.text: Safari sends no event at all when the pointer leaves for another window -- measured against the macOS Accessibility Keyboard, which floats over the page and never takes focus. No pointerout, no pointerleave, no blur; :hover stays true and the dwell underneath fires into an empty room.
A tracked pointer emits a move every ~33ms even while its owner holds still, so silence from one of those means it has gone. A mouse is silent at rest and is deliberately untouched by any of this.

commits.subject: Grow the message box with what is in it

body.text: It was one line, fixed, with the overflow scrolled and the scrollbar hidden — so a message longer than the box went above the fold and stayed there. Every other surface in this app has dwell controls for scrolling; this one has none and nothing to hang them on, so what scrolls out of it is gone as far as a gaze user is concerned.

Measured rather than counted: a line is however many characters fit at this text size and this width, which is not a number the app can know. The height is cleared before each measurement, or the box only ever grows — `scrollHeight` includes whatever room it is already being given.

The cap stays in the stylesheet, in rem and dvh, at five lines or a third of a short screen, whichever is less. The board underneath is what somebody is speaking with, and a message box that ate it would be a box with nothing to put in it.
Where nothing can be measured, nothing is set: the same fallback the grid's windowing makes, and a box set to nought is a box nobody can see.

commits.subject: Icons for show and copy, and the two ways to stop side by side

body.text: Show and copy become an eye and a copy button. The field beside them is the widest thing in the panel, and two labelled buttons pushed it down to nothing on a phone. The name stays on each of them: an icon says nothing aloud, and these are the two controls where picking the wrong one either puts a credential on a shared screen or fails to copy it at all.

Turn on is Start. Turn off is Stop, and it moves down beside 'Stop and erase the copy' — the two that stop it, in that order, so the larger of them is never the one nearer to hand. Stop leaves the copy where it is for the other devices; the one beside it takes that away too.
Stop is offered in the choose state as well, which is new. Without it the only way past a question somebody does not want to answer was to leave the panel, and it was waiting again next time.

commits.subject: Leave text size and volume on the device, and settle after the screen moves

body.text: Two things, both about a device rather than a person.

Text size and volume belong to the screen and the speaker in front of somebody — a phone at arm's length and a tablet on a wheelchair mount want different numbers, and it is the same person. So they are blanked on the way out and this device's own kept on the way in. Blanked as well as ignored, or turning the text size up would count as news and arrive on the other device as "board updated from your other device", a notice about something that did not happen. A backup still carries both: restoring one is putting a device back, which is a different question.

And a pointer rests where it last fired. Whatever arrives underneath gets a pointerenter of its own, so a control appearing under a resting pointer starts dwelling on nobody's instruction. The menu has guarded its own items from the start; `holdDwells` is that second applied where the whole screen changes — leaving a panel, and changing the text size, which relays out every control around a pointer that has not moved.
It stops controls arming and leaves a control already being held alone. A test caught the version that cancelled: it made the text-size spinner step once and stop instead of repeating while held.

The wire format moves to `core/envelope.ts` on the way, because taking one value from the store put `core/phrases` in the Netlify function and turned a 3KB Lambda into 418KB of phrase table. It imports nothing now, and the structure test says so.

commits.subject: Carry the ElevenLabs account between a user's own devices

body.text: The key is kept out of a backup because a backup is a file made to be handed to somebody else, and the key in one hands over the account. A sync snapshot is a different question: it is sealed with the user's own passphrase and reaches their own devices and nowhere else.
So the account rides *beside* the backup, in `Snapshot.account`. Inside it, every exported file would carry it too — and that rule is written in four places and tested in one.

Three states, not two. An account, an explicit null meaning unlink, and absent, meaning a snapshot written before this existed said nothing. Silence must not be read as an unlink or one device on an older release strips the account off all of them.

`settings.voiceURI` already travelled, so a phrase given an ElevenLabs voice on one device arrived on the next naming a voice it could not fetch, and fell back to the device voice. Now the account arrives with it.
The account moves up to `talk.tsx` on the way: it is part of what sync sends, and a settings row holding its own copy goes stale the moment a board arrives carrying a different one.

commits.subject: Show and copy the passphrase and the API key

body.text: Both were write-only. The passphrase is wanted on the *second* device and nobody — including us — can work it out from anything else, so a board whose passphrase was forgotten was a board that could not be reached. ElevenLabs shows a key exactly once, which made the same problem out of a second device wanting the same account.

One `SecretField` serves both rows: hidden by default, and **copyable without ever being shown**, which is the usual case — it is wanted on the other device rather than on this screen. Showing it is a second deliberate act, because this panel spans the viewport and these are set up in rooms with other people in them. It does not re-hide on a timer: somebody reading a passphrase out to whoever holds the second device needs it to stay where it is.
A refusal from the clipboard is said out loud rather than swallowed — writing it needs permission, and a dwell is a timer with no key press in it.

commits.subject: Deploy the sync function, and notice when it is not there

body.text: `/api/sync` on production answered 200 with the app's own HTML: the function was never deployed. The build was green, because nothing about a missing function fails a build — Netlify simply did not pick up a `.mts` file, and the SPA catch-all rewrote the path to index.html.
So it is `.ts` now, which is what every Netlify TypeScript function is, and `@netlify/blobs` moves to dependencies, which is what it is: the deployed function imports it at runtime.

The second half is the part worth keeping. A missing endpoint here is not a 404 — the catch-all makes it a 200 with a document in it, which is the one failure shape a client checking `res.ok` cannot see, and the first `{` it looked for threw inside the one part of Peri that is supposed to fail into a line of text. The client now refuses an answer that is not JSON and says the service is not available, which is true.

commits.subject: Move every test under tests/, mirroring the tree it covers

body.text: Netlify publishes every file in netlify/functions/ as a function, so the test beside the handler was deployed as one and took the build down. The fix for that alone is one file, but a rule with one exception is a rule somebody forgets — so all twenty-five move, and structure.test.ts fails if a .test.ts appears under src/ or netlify/ again.

Tests beside the code is the nicer arrangement and this gives it up for a reason that is not taste: what ships and what checks it are now two trees that cannot be confused for each other by a bundler.

The layering rule no longer covers tests, because they are no longer in the tree it describes — which is what it was always for. Tailwind's scan loses its test exclusion for the same reason: there is nothing to exclude from a scan rooted at src.

commits.subject: Synchronize two devices through a box neither we nor anyone can open

body.text: Peri had no backend and said so in four places. Synchronizing needs somewhere to put a board, so it now has one: a Netlify function over Blobs, holding ciphertext at an address it cannot connect to a person.

One passphrase does two jobs. PBKDF2 salted with the account gives a master; HKDF expands it into the AES-GCM key the board is sealed with and the 64-hex address it is stored under. So the address *is* the credential: a server holding it cannot derive the key, and somebody who does not know the passphrase cannot find the blob at all. The alternative was keeping OAuth tokens on every device to prove an account server-side, which is a worse thing to leave on a tablet in a day room.

The payload is a backup — the document that already exists, is already a diff against the phrase table, and is already tested against damage. Built at a fixed epoch, because a stamp that moves every render is a board that looks edited every render.

The last change wins, whole; merging half of one diff into half of another is a board neither device ever had, and between your own devices a deletion has to travel. The exception is the first exchange, where clocks are worthless: nothing on the server and this device publishes, nothing of the user's here and it takes what is there, both and it asks and touches neither until answered.

The service worker serves every same-origin GET from cache first, which is right for build artefacts and would have pinned every device to the board it held this morning. /api/ is exempt, and a test says so.

The privacy policy said "we operate no servers". Its own test failed rather than letting that go stale, and it now says what we hold, what we can see of it, and what nobody can do for you if the passphrase is lost.

commits.subject: Say the hold's shape once, in the repeat rather than in the body

body.text: The body branched on `selectOnHold` as well, and a mutation showed it could not matter: without the option there is no repeat, so the step never leaves nought however the body is written. Kept where it is observable, and a run of spaces now has a test — the caret takes the word behind it rather than selecting nothing at all.

commits.subject: Put back a deleted list, and drive every field in the panel by dwell

body.text: Deleting a list is the largest loss this panel hands out — fifty words in one dwell, and every phrase that named it left with a blank — so the undo beside the + and the pencil puts the last one back. What goes back is the state the name was in, not the words that were on show: a list the table ships that nobody had touched is un-hidden and stores nothing, or it would be pinned to this release and stop following the table.

Every box in the panel now takes the caret from where somebody rests, the way the message box does — a box you cannot put a caret into is one you can only clear and retype. Selecting is the part a dwell could not say at all: a rest says "here" and a selection is two things, so the second is said by not moving. Rest, and the caret lands; keep resting, and the word around it goes; once more, and the whole box does. The fill replays for each step and stops when there is nothing left to take.
The message box opts out. A pointer parked over the message while its owner reads the board is at rest without meaning anything by it.

commits.subject: Release a held word in one place rather than two

body.text: The pencil released as well, and a mutation showed it could not matter: the only way back into arranging is the arrange toggle, which releases on the way in. Dead code with a comment claiming a purpose it has not got is worse than no code, so the release stays where it is reachable and the pencil says why it needs none.

commits.subject: Edit a list's words behind a pencil, and put back what was deleted

body.text: The × sat on every chip in every state, which is a delete under the pointer of somebody reading their own words — and a gaze that rests is a gaze that fires. A chip is now one of three things and never two: text to read, a field with an × beside it, or something to pick up and put down. The two modes turn each other off, and closing the list puts both away.

Deleting is the one edit with nothing to show for it afterwards, so every removal is kept with the index it had in the stored order and the undo beside the pencil splices it back there — the stored order, not the one on show, or an undo out of A–Z rearranges the list it is repairing.
A word keeps the case it is typed in. A list's name is the key a slot looks up and still folds to lower case; one field serves both and takes the difference as a prop.

commits.subject: Bound the aliases panel, and start every list closed

body.text: The panel borrowed `.settings-panel`, which fills whatever height it is given — right for Settings, which is given the viewport, and wrong here. Hanging from the menu, this one is given the height of its own lists, and a pane told to fill that can never overflow: no arrows, and everything past the bottom of the screen out of reach, there being no wheel and no scrollbar. `.alias-panel` bounds it in `dvh`, as Backup bounds itself.

Every list is closed on arrival now, so what you land on is ten names rather than one list already unrolled. The guide's headings still open their first section, and the difference is deliberate: a guide is opened to read something, this is opened to reach one list out of ten.

commits.subject: Let every list be renamed and deleted, the table's included

body.text: A list the table ships cannot be deleted by leaving it out of the store — the table puts it straight back on the next render — so the store gains a `hidden` set beside the lists, for the same reason `PhraseStore.hidden` exists. `aliasOverlay` turns a hidden name into an *empty* list rather than a missing one: present-but-empty is what stops the lookup falling through to the table, which is the whole of what deleting one has to mean.

Renaming a shipped list is built out of the same thing — the words move to the new name and the old one is hidden. The phrases that said {pronouns} then resolve to a blank, which is the cost of it and the user's call to make about their own board.
A merge never applies `hidden`, exactly as it never applies a phrase removal: a file somebody else made must not take a list off your device. Replace does.

Two older shapes are still read. `readAliases` takes either `{ lists, hidden }` or the bare record of lists the store was until now, which is what a backup written in between carries — and an old `dwellspeak_profile` is folded in as it already was.

commits.subject: Add a list from a +, and name one from an edit toggle

body.text: Two controls above the lists, since they are about the lists rather than about any one list's words: a + that adds one, and an edit toggle that turns every heading into a name field with a delete beside it. The row that used to sit at the bottom asking for a name before it would make anything is gone.

The + cannot ask for a name — it is one dwell, and naming is a keyboard job — so it makes `new-list`, opens it, and switches the naming mode on so the field is already there to type in. A second one is `new-list-2`. A name is committed on Enter or on leaving the field rather than per keystroke: a rename is a change of key, and rewriting it letter by letter would leave lists called "d", "dr", "dri", taking the focus with them each time.

Only a list the user made can be renamed or deleted. A name the table ships is written into the phrases that use it — rename `pronouns` and every phrase saying {pronouns} quietly resolves to nothing — so those are shown and not offered, and the toggle stays disabled until there is a list of their own.
Delete moves out of the open list's toolbar and onto the heading, beside the name it deletes; the toolbar is left with the two controls that act on words.

commits.subject: Fold the alias lists, and let each one be arranged

body.text: The panel was nine lists laid out end to end, `bodyparts` alone being fifty words to scroll past to reach the one you came for. They fold now: one open at a time, the first open on arrival, and opening one puts its heading at the top of the pane — the same bargain the guide's headings strike. A closed list is unmounted rather than hidden, or a screen reader reads out three hundred words nobody asked for.

The open one draws its words as a grid, sized in `ch` so a column holds a word, and carries the two arrangements the category tabs offer: A to Z, or the order the words were put in. A to Z is a view — the order underneath is left alone, so going to A to Z and back is not a way to lose an arrangement — and which one is showing is kept under its own small key, since the order is content and the view of it is not.

Arranging comes out of `ui/reorder`, so a word is picked up by one dwell and put down by another, exactly as a category tab is. A move made while A to Z is showing captures the order that was on screen and becomes the user's own, the way `reorderCategories` does; a move applied to the hidden order would land somewhere they could not see.

A chip is never both a remove and a handle. Two targets in one place is the worst thing to hand somebody aiming by gaze, and a dwell meant to put a word down would delete it — so arranging replaces the ×, and closing the list puts down whatever is in the air.
`SortAlphaIcon` and `CustomOrderIcon` move to `ui/icons.tsx`, now that two surfaces draw them.

commits.subject: Take four duplicates out of the table, and refuse a fifth

body.text: Four phrases were listed twice in the same category — "I am getting along", "Not very good today", "Thank you for being such a good friend" and "That's my problem". The rows differ only in the table's own `id` field, which this app ignores, and the disambiguating suffix in `makePhrase` gave the second copy a working id, so they have been on the board for years as two cells saying the same thing.

The same wording under *different* categories stays: "Good morning" is under Interpersonal, Texting and Time of Day, and somebody looks in whichever of the three they think in. Taking those out would empty three categories of their most-used phrases.

Adding one is refused the same way. Save goes quiet and the strip says "Already on the board" — a control that has gone quiet explains nothing by itself. Matched on the source, folded to lower case with its spaces collapsed, within a category only, and a phrase never duplicates itself: a phrase opened to fix a typo has to be savable.
`core/phrases.test.ts` holds the table to it, so the fifth cannot arrive the way the first four did.

commits.subject: Replace My details with Aliases, seeded from the table

body.text: An alias is a named list of words a phrase's slot chooses from. The table ships nine — pronouns, directions, body parts and friends — and two of them arrive empty, `contacts` and `name`, because there is nowhere in the data to put a particular person. My details edited exactly those two and nothing else, which made the other seven a thing only the source could change.

All of them are the user's now. The panel is seeded from the table, every word can come off, every list can be added to, and a list of their own is a name and a `+` away — reached from a phrase by writing that name in curly brackets. Only what they touched is stored, so a list nobody has been near follows the table into the next release.
A key that is present wins outright, an empty list included. Falling back to the shipped words would make taking the last word off a list the one edit the panel could not carry out.

`Profile` is gone, and with it `profileAliases` — the name and contacts were always these same lists behind the scenes. An old profile is folded into aliases the first time `loadAliases` finds no alias store, and a backup written before this carries `profile` where the new one carries `aliases`; `parseBackup` reads both. Renaming a menu item must not lose somebody their contacts.
Merging a backup adds and never takes away, for the reason merging phrases does: a file somebody else made must not be able to delete a word off a list on your device.

commits.subject: Lift the muted grey to 7:1 on every surface

body.text: --text-muted carries every sublabel, hint and count in the app, and it was #888: 4.7:1 against a cell and 4.3:1 against one being hovered — under what AA asks for, in the one state a control is in while somebody is reading it.
#b0b0b0 clears 7:1 against all four surfaces, hover included, which is what AAA asks and what an app read by people with low vision should hold.
The arithmetic is in structure.test.ts rather than in anybody's eye, and it reads the palette out of the stylesheet — so it fails if the grey is dimmed again or if a surface is lightened past it.

commits.subject: Size text in rem, and add a zoom setting

body.text: Every font-size in the stylesheet was a pixel count — 77 of them across seventeen sizes, plus four written inline in the menu — so nothing could change them all at once. They are one scale now, 0.8rem to 2.5rem, with the app's normal text at 1rem. 1rem is the browser's own default rather than a number this app picked, so ordinary text is 16px where it was 13, and a reader who has already told their browser they want larger text gets it.

The geometry that bounds text moves to rem with it: the message box and the icon buttons beside it, the edit strip and its inset, the grid cell's minimum height, and the topbar padding that anchors the mode strip. A box fixed in pixels around text that scales is a box that clips the moment somebody turns the zoom up. Spacing that holds nothing stays in pixels.

Text size is the first row in Settings — it is the setting somebody needs before they can read the others, including that panel — and it is applied as the root font-size, as a percentage, so it multiplies what the browser was already doing rather than replacing it. Half again as small to twice as large; a file cannot import a value outside that, which would take the settings panel down with it.

`src/structure.test.ts` fails on any font-size left in pixels, in the stylesheet or in a component. A single one left behind is a line that will not grow for the person who went looking for this setting, and 77 of them show nothing in a diff.

commits.subject: Take --danger back to #ef4444

body.text: The same red the five destructive controls were already drawn in, now said once. #bd1e06 read at 2.8:1 against the panel surface, and Delete, Sign out and Reset are labels rather than fills.

commits.subject: Say destruction in --danger, and put the menu items back

body.text: Every red left in the stylesheet was #ef4444 written out by hand, in five places and in four notations — a hex, two rgba() alphas and a color-mix. They all read --danger now, so the palette says what it means: --danger is destruction, --urgent is the emergency bar, and nothing outside those two ideas is red anywhere.
Also restores the narrowed menu items, which the last commit reverted by mistake, along with their test and note.

commits.subject: Let the menu items span the panel again

body.text: Reverting the narrowed hit area, along with the test and the note that described it. The one-second guard after an item closes stays.

commits.subject: Give the emergency bar its own colour, out of a token

body.text: --urgent, and the bar reads from it everywhere it used to hard-code a red. --danger is declared alongside it for the reds that are about destroying something rather than about urgency; nothing reads it yet.

commits.subject: Narrow the menu items, and go deaf for a second after one closes

body.text: The items stretched the panel, which spans the viewport — so a row of text a few centimetres long answered to a gaze anywhere along a metre of empty space beside it, and the five of them tiled the panel with no gap between one and the next. Shrunk to their content they are five targets with somewhere safe to look in between.

And a pointer rests where it last fired. Back sits over the menu that comes back, and the sign-out dialog's buttons are centred squarely over it, so an item arriving under a pointer already at rest opens on its own — possibly the item that raised the dialog. The menu ignores a dwell for a second afterwards. Nothing about the items changes while it does: five rows greying out and coming back reads as a fault rather than as a pause, so the cue is that the fill does not start.

commits.subject: Drop the grid's page controls on a short screen

body.text: Six controls stacked in a column need vertical room, and a phone on its side has none to spare. The pages are the pair that goes: a nudge repeats while it is held, so it crosses the same distance a page does, and the two ends still reach either end of the grid in one dwell. Nothing becomes unreachable.

Height alone is the test, with no orientation clause. The category bar's rule needs one because a tablet in portrait is wider than a phone; here a landscape tablet is 768px tall against a landscape phone's 430px, so the height already tells them apart.

commits.subject: Tighten the padding around the emergency bar

body.text: 1.5rem to 1rem, which gives the grid 16px back without moving any of the buttons relative to each other.

commits.subject: One line around the message box, not two

body.text: Edit mode drew a dashed outline on the box, which already has a border of its own — and an outline sits just outside the border, so the two read as a double line around a single box. The mode is drawn on the border itself now: dashed and accent-tinted, the same cue the phrase cells carry.
The focus colour is restated at the same specificity, so a focused box still brightens. The style says which mode the board is in, the colour says where the typing will go.

commits.subject: Open talking, with the caret already in the box

body.text: Auto-speak shipped on, but only for somebody who had never used Peri: it is saved with every other setting, so anyone with a stored `false` — which is everyone who has used the app — kept getting a silent board. It is a mode rather than a preference, so it is now ignored on the way back in and every load starts in it. Switching out is two dwells; a board that cannot say anything the moment it is switched on is not recoverable the same way.

The message box takes `autoFocus` with it, so somebody with a keyboard can type the first thing they want to say without having to place the caret first — which is the one thing a dwell could not do at all until the box grew a dwell of its own. A programmatic focus does not raise a phone's on-screen keyboard, which needs a real gesture.
Tests about composing now switch out of auto-speak after rendering rather than seeding it off, since seeding it no longer does anything.

commits.subject: Put the edit strip back on the border it rides

body.text: It was centred 20px below it. The strip's `bottom` and the topbar's padding-bottom have to be the same number — one is where the message box's lower border falls, the other is where the strip's own centre line falls — and they were written as two. The padding then grew to 30px to make room for the strip while the strip stayed at 10px, so it floated in the gap under the box instead of straddling its border.

One `--edit-bar-inset` now, used in both places, and set to half the strip's stated height so its lower edge reaches the bottom of the bar and no further. Stating the height is what makes half of it a number rather than a guess.
A test reads the two out of index.css and asserts they agree — jsdom applies no cascade, so that is as far as it goes, but it is the drift that caused this rather than the geometry.

commits.subject: A strip on each border, and three modes in a ring

body.text: The category and the voice move onto the lower border of the message box, centred on it exactly as the modes are on the upper one — so a phrase's two other properties belong to the box holding its words rather than to a band underneath it. Rendered by the topbar now, since that is what it is positioned against; `.edit-bar` bottom matches the bar's padding-bottom, and edit mode adds half the strip's height to that padding so the lower half does not hang over the category tabs.

Auto-speak ships on, so opening Peri for the first time is enough to be able to say something. And the two toggles now reach all three states in a ring: switching auto-speak off is a request to change the phrases, so it lands in edit mode, and switching edit off comes back to composing. `setMode` is the only thing that writes any of it.

Every test that composes a phrase into the box now says `{ autoSpeak: false }` for itself, and `readSettings` falls a missing auto-speak back to the default rather than to false — a file that says nothing about a setting is a file that says nothing.

commits.subject: Say what the editor is now, in the guide and in AGENTS.md

body.text: Both described a dialog that no longer exists. The guide gains what edit mode now does — the box is where phrases are written, the tick saves, the bin deletes, and auto-speak switches off while it is on — and AGENTS.md gains a section for the arrangement, plus the two rules that are easy to undo by accident: the message and the draft are separate, and the grid does not narrow itself to the draft.

commits.subject: Edit phrases in the message box, not in a dialog

body.text: The phrase editor was a dialog, which is the wrong shape for a board driven by gaze: it covered the very phrases being edited, it had to be got out of before anything else could be reached, and every one of its controls was a target somewhere the pointer had never been.

So in edit mode the message box *is* the editor. There is always a draft; choosing a phrase points the draft at it rather than opening anything. The rail beside the box changes with the mode — speak, copy and paste become save, delete and paste, in the same three places — and a strip under it carries the two things a phrase has besides its words: its category and its voice. The category is chosen from the same full-screen grid the voice is, which is the only shape of "one out of many" a dwell can work; it was a native `<select>`, whose list the operating system draws where nothing can be hovered at all.

Edit and auto-speak are exclusive now. They ask opposite things of the same dwell — one makes a phrase a thing to say this instant, the other a thing to rewrite — so switching either on switches the other off.

Two things fall out of it. A brand-new phrase now keeps the voice chosen for it: `addPhrase` hands back the id it makes, and until the phrase exists there is nothing to hang a voice on, so the choice used to be dropped. And the grid no longer narrows itself to the word being typed while a phrase is being written, which would take away the phrases somebody came to edit.

commits.subject: Close the gap between the guide's headings

body.text: Folded up they are a list, and the border under each is what keeps one off the next — so the 20px between sections is a gap with nothing to do.

Scoped to the collapsible ones rather than taken off `.help-section`, which also draws the privacy policy and the terms. Those have no borders and rely on that margin; without it their sections run together. Two classes also beats the `:first-of-type` rule, so the first heading sits flush like the rest.

commits.subject: Offer a paste control in both text boxes

body.text: The keyboard route into a text box is Ctrl-V, which is the one input this whole app exists without — so a control asks on the user's behalf. Beside Copy in the message box, since they are the pair, and under the text in the phrase editor, where a pointer travelling to it crosses neither Save nor Delete.
It gets the same treatment a keyboard paste does: an address becomes the name of the page, and it lands at the caret rather than at the end.

It can be refused, and for the people this app is for refusal is the likely case rather than the unlikely one. Reading the clipboard needs permission and, in most browsers, a recent click or key press — and a dwell is a timer firing after a pointer has rested, with no press anywhere in it. Firefox does not offer it to a page at all. So `pasteFromClipboard` says which of three things happened and the screen says it out loud, the same bargain `openLink` strikes and for the same reason: silence would leave the control looking simply broken.
Never disabled, unlike Speak and Copy. What is on the clipboard is not this app's to know until it asks, so a paste with nothing behind it says so rather than being greyed out on a guess.
The guide says all of this, including what to do on Firefox. Writing it tripped the guide's own limit on how long a paragraph may be, which is the test doing its job.

commits.subject: Tighten the guide's headings, and open one at the top of the pane

body.text: The padding goes. Folded up the guide is a list of headings, and the tighter that list is the more of it is on screen at once, which is the point of folding it. The row is still full width, so what shrinks is the height of the target rather than its area, and the border below each is what keeps one off the next.

Opening a section now scrolls its heading to the top of the pane. Opening one low in the list used to leave the heading where it was and the text it had just revealed below the fold — so the reader had to go and find the scroll arrows to see the thing they had asked for. It runs in an effect after the render that opened it, so the layout it scrolls to is the one with this section already expanded and the previous one already closed.
Closing does not scroll: closing is not going anywhere, and moving the page under somebody who has just finished reading is its own annoyance.
jsdom implements no `scrollIntoView` at all — a missing function rather than one that quietly does nothing — so the setup stubs it and records what asked, which is also what the two new tests read.

commits.subject: An opaque mode strip, taller panels, and a guide that folds up

body.text: The strip carrying edit, Rest and auto-speak sits on the message box, and with nothing behind it the box's border and whatever had been typed showed through the gaps between the three. It is opaque black now, in a lozenge of its own, and sits above everything in the app — below the panel and the dialogs, which are meant to cover it. Its own padding makes it 32px tall, so the topbar's padding and the strip's `top` both go to 16px to keep it centred on the border.

Settings and the guide fill the viewport; the menu and the shorter panels still hang down only as far as their content. Both of those two are scrolled whatever height they get, and a taller pane is fewer dwells on the scroll arrows. Sized in `dvh`, because on a phone `vh` is the viewport with the browser chrome hidden and the last row of a panel measured in it cannot be reached.

The guide gains an overview, the syntax for writing a phrase with choices, and the formatting a phrase can carry — the first for somebody arriving, the other two for whoever writes the phrases. It also stopped sending people to the right-hand column for the edit and auto-speak buttons, which have not been there since they moved to the strip.

Its headings fold up, one open at a time, the first open on arrival: fifteen sections is a lot to scroll past by dwell to reach the one you came for. A closed section is unmounted rather than hidden, so a screen reader is not read out the whole guide. The legal pages are the same shape of text drawn by the same component and deliberately do not fold — they are documents, served at their own URLs and indexed.

commits.subject: Give every setting a revert, and Settings a factory reset

body.text: Auto-repeat now defaults to 1000ms. Its ceiling goes up with it, from 1000 to 2000: a default sitting on its own limit leaves half the spinner inert, which reads as broken, and somebody who wants a whole second between repeats may well want more.

Every settable value gains a revert at the end of its spinner, naming what it goes back to. It goes quiet at the default rather than away — a row that changed width as a value crossed its default would move the two buttons beside it, and a control somebody has learnt to find should be in the same place whether or not it has anything to do. `ResetIcon` is a closed loop rather than the open hook `UndoIcon` draws: Undo is in the topbar and means the last thing done to a message, and the two must not be learnt as one control.

Reset to Factory Defaults takes everything, not only the settings, so it asks first — portalled and centred like the Sign-out confirmation, since a pointer rests where it last fired and a "yes" under it would answer itself. The dialog leads with a backup to keep: deleting a phrase is the one change with no road back and this deletes all of them at once. It says a file was saved only once the browser has taken it. Signing out stays its own item, so a reset leaves the user signed in.

The reset clears storage and reloads. Nothing in that panel can reach the React state holding the same values — the board, the composer, the sent list, its own account row — and a screen still offering phrases that no longer exist is worse than no reset at all. The keys are listed rather than `localStorage.clear()`: the origin may hold something Peri did not put there, and a reset is no licence to remove somebody else's.
The download moves out of the backup panel to `menu/backup-file.ts`, now that two places offer to save one.

commits.subject: Repeat the page controls, and drop the bar's ends on a portrait phone

body.text: Paging repeats while held now, like the nudges and at the same `repeatDelayMs`. I had argued the other way — repeats of a whole screen queue their smooth scrolls, so holding it travels fast — but the pace is the user's to set, which is the answer to that.

The category bar's two end arrows are hidden on a phone held upright. Six arrows and the tools leave a portrait phone almost no room for the tabs they exist to reach, and the ends are the ones to lose: paging reaches either end as well, only a screen at a time, whereas nothing else nudges. Width alone is not the test — a tablet in portrait is over 700px and keeps all six.

Also fixes something the page controls broke without my noticing. The arrow dividers were `:last-child` and `:nth-last-child(2)`, written when there were two arrows to the right of the tabs; adding the pages made three, and the portrait rule makes two, so counting from the end was always going to keep being wrong. They key off which side of the scroller an arrow sits on instead.

The portrait rule is asserted against the text of the stylesheet, which is as far as jsdom reaches: it applies no cascade and lays nothing out, so whether the rule takes effect is a question for the preview.

commits.subject: Add next/previous page to the rail and the category bar

body.text: Both surfaces had a nudge and a jump to either end, and nothing in between. Nudging 120px at a time down two thousand phrases is a long way, and jumping to the bottom overshoots everything you were reading towards. A page is the step that was missing.

Three sizes of jump now sit on each bar, and a gaze user has to tell them apart without reading: one chevron nudges, two chevrons move a screen, a chevron against a bar goes to the end. They are ordered outward by how far they travel, so position says it as well as the glyph does. `PageIcon` lives in `ui/icons` for the same reason `ReorderIcon` does — both bars that can be paged draw it.

A page is the visible extent *less one nudge's worth*, not the whole extent. Grid rows are not a uniform height, and category tabs are pills of every width, so a jump of exactly one screen leaves something cut across the fold — a phrase half off the top, or half a category at the edge that a gaze user hits meaning its neighbour. The floor keeps a viewport smaller than the overlap from paging by nothing at all.
It does not repeat, alone among the held controls. Repeats of a whole screen queue their smooth scrolls into a blur, and the point of a page is knowing where you landed.

commits.subject: Make the auto-repeat delay a setting, and unbinarise backup.ts

body.text: How long between repeats while a control is held — the scroll nudges, the filter arrows, the settings spinners. It was two hardcoded numbers, 180 in two places and 200 in two others, with nothing recording why they differed; all four now read `settings.repeatDelayMs`, which unifies them at 200 and makes the scroll nudges 20ms slower than they were.

Held apart from the dwell time because the two answer different questions. The dwell is how long somebody needs to settle on a target; this is how fast they travel once they have. A slow, deliberate gaze may want a long dwell and quick repeats, and that combination was not expressible before.

The floor of 100ms is not a matter of taste. A repeat fast enough to outrun a gaze user's reaction turns a nudge into a jump to the end of the list — and the control they would reach for to slow it down repeats at the same rate. `readSettings` clamps an imported value to the same range, which it had to be told about: it builds the object field by field, so a new setting is a compiler error there rather than a silent omission.

Bundled with it, because it is what made finding that clamp difficult: `core/backup.ts` held a raw NUL byte as the separator in a composite map key, which made the whole file *binary* to grep — and a search over a binary file answers nothing rather than saying it cannot. Every search across this tree has been skipping that file in silence. The character is the right separator, being the one thing no category name or phrase can contain, so it stays; it is written as an escape now. `structure.test.ts` fails on any source file carrying one, which it did for this commit's own first draft.

commits.subject: Ride the mode strip on the message box's top border

body.text: Centred on that border in both directions rather than sitting in a band above it. `top` matches the topbar's padding, which is where the border is, and the translate takes back half the strip's own height; the padding has to be at least half a toggle or the strip overflows the top of the bar, which is why 1.5rem toggles make it 12px.

The band cost the grid 18px. This costs 2px. What it costs instead is the top-centre of the message box, which now answers to a mode rather than to the caret — and by more than it looks, since the toggles carry invisible hit areas 8px wider than they are painted. Rest was already sitting there, so that surface was never entirely the box's.

commits.subject: Put all three modes in one strip across the top

body.text: Edit and auto-speak come up out of the grid rail to sit either side of Rest: edit left, auto-speak right. They are the same kind of thing as Rest — a mode, on or off, not an action — and the middle of the screen's top is where a gaze on its way anywhere passes, which is worth more to a mode than the head of a rail is. The rail is left to scrolling.
Rest keeps the centre. It is the one control that has to be findable without looking, and it was found there.

This costs the grid 18px. Rest alone was half a rem tall and needed almost no strip; two icons beside it need one they can be seen in, so the topbar's top padding goes from 10px to 28px. The alternative was letting them overlap the message box, which would put a mode toggle on top of the one surface a message is typed into. The old comment claiming Rest takes no height from the grid is no longer true and no longer says so.

The tests picked these two out of the rail by position — `toggles()[1]` was edit in thirty places — and the order is now reversed, so they ask for them by name instead. `.toggle-btn` carried rail geometry that has no meaning here and is gone; `.edit-toggle` and `.autospeak-toggle` are what both the stylesheet and the tests reach for.

commits.subject: Give the emergency tools the category tools' box

body.text: They were 84px wide and stretched to whatever height the phrases came to — a tile's worth of room on this bar of all bars, spent on something with no words in it. And it made the rising dwell wash a tall column here and a small lozenge there, off the same two icons.

46 by 36 now, the category tools to the pixel, centred rather than stretched so a phrase long enough to wrap does not drag them taller with it. The narrow-screen concession goes with it: 84px halved to 48px there because two fixed-width tools beside six phrases was a lot of bar, and 46px at every width is narrower than the concession was.

The pair also sits 6px apart, as the category pair does. They are direct children of the bar and take its 1.5rem gap like the phrases, and there is no wrapper to give them a gap of their own, so the second pulls itself back by the difference. Only the second — the space between the phrases and the pair is the bar's rhythm.

commits.subject: One icon size for both bars, and a wash that rises

body.text: The four tool glyphs are the same four glyphs at either end of the screen, so they are held to one size rather than each tuned to its own bar: 1.2rem, 1rem under 700px. In rem, so they track the text beside them rather than sitting at a fixed pixel count next to it.
Borders are transparent in every state now, `is-on` included. The filled mode still reads as filled without one.

The dwell fills bottom up rather than left to right, which is what the topbar icon buttons already do — `dwellFillV`, an inset wash in `--accent-dim`, scaled from the bottom edge. A 3px line along the bottom reads as an underline on something with an edge to underline, and with the pill gone there is nothing for it to sit under. Translucent so the glyph stays legible through it, and the emergency tools take the accent rather than the red: they are tools beside that bar, not phrases on it.
The base rule sizes a dwell bar as a 3px sliver, and `width: 0` beats `inset` at deciding how wide a box is, so both have to be undone by hand.

commits.subject: Draw the bar tools as bare glyphs

body.text: The add, sort and reorder controls on the category bar and the emergency bar were bordered, padded chips. On the category bar that put a pill at the end of a row of pills, and on the emergency bar a tile in a row of tiles — so the two controls a user has to pick out without reading the bar were drawn as the thing they had to be picked out from.

Border and padding go. The icons carry it instead: heavier stroke, and larger, set in CSS rather than in the markup because `PlusIcon` is also the add control in the profile panel and wants an ordinary weight there.

Three things kept deliberately. The hit area, now sized rather than padded and set to what the padding came to, so neither bar changes height. The border, transparent, because `is-on` gives it a colour and a border appearing from nothing would shift the glyph a pixel each time the mode was switched. And the filled `is-on` state, which is the only thing on either bar announcing that tabs have become things to pick up.
The emergency tools no longer take the red wash on dwell. They are the tools beside the bar, not something to say out loud, and the tint was the one cue claiming otherwise.

commits.subject: Hold the caret reporting where a test can actually see it

body.text: The grid-filter test passes with `onPlace` pulled out, because jsdom answers `setSelectionRange` with a `selectionchange` that React turns into `onSelect` — already wired to the same setter. Through the app the two paths are indistinguishable, so the claim moves to the hook, where it is one call and one assertion.

Keeping the explicit call rather than leaning on the synthetic event: `selectionchange` on a form control is a late addition, and a browser that does not fire it leaves the grid completing a word the caret has left, silently, looking exactly like a broken search.
The app-level test stays for the outcome and now says what it cannot isolate, so the next person does not read it as covering the wiring.

commits.subject: Place the caret by dwell in the message box too

body.text: The message box had a dwell already, but it only moved focus there, and it switched itself off the moment the box held focus — so the caret could be placed exactly once, on the way in, and never again. That gate was protecting something real: a pointer parked on the box while its owner types must not sit there firing. Aiming is what settles it instead. A pointer that has not moved does not re-arm, focus or no focus, so the dwell can stay live for as long as the box is in use.

The caret matters more here than in the phrase editor. It decides which word the grid narrows itself to, and it is tracked in state rather than read off the box, so the hook reports where it put the caret and the composer is told — otherwise the grid goes on completing a word the caret has left.
Both boxes now want the same dwell, so it moves to `ui/caret` as `useCaretDwell` and the editor's copy goes. `focus`, `focused` and `setFocused` go with it: the gate was their only reader.

commits.subject: Write down which position the aim is measured from

body.text: The trap is that measuring each movement against the one before it looks equivalent to measuring from where the wait began, and is not. Said in `movedAway`, where the argument is passed, and in the guide beside the note about testing it — which now also says a single big jump passes either way, since that is what let this through.

commits.subject: Measure aiming from where the wait began, not from the last movement

body.text: A pointer does not jump. It crosses the phrase box as a stream of small movements, and the re-arm threshold was measured against the one before rather than against where the wait began — so a pointer could travel the whole phrase in three-pixel steps without a single step counting. The dwell never re-armed, and leaving the box and coming back was the only way to place the caret a second time.

Two positions now: where the pointer is, which is what the caret is placed by, and where the current wait began, which is what the distance is measured from. The existing test moved sixty pixels in one event and so passed either way; the new one takes the same journey in fours.

The fill on the box is restarted by hand at the same moment. Every other control remounts its bar to do that, but a textarea can hold no children, so its fill is an animation on the box itself — and re-arming does not change the class, leaving the bar promising a firing no longer coming.

commits.subject: Test the re-arm with a move rather than a re-entry, and write it down

body.text: A pointer travelling within an element fires only pointermove. The test fired pointerenter too, which re-arms the dwell by itself — so it passed with the re-arming taken out.

commits.subject: Let the caret be placed in a phrase by dwell

body.text: A text box was the one control dwell alone could not drive. Hovering could focus it, but the caret only moved when something was clicked, and a click is the input a gaze user does not have. Typing comes from whatever keyboard they already use; saying where to type is the part no keyboard supplies.

Dwelling over the phrase text now asks the browser which character is under the pointer and puts the caret there, re-arming when the pointer aims somewhere new — a dwell fires once on arrival, so otherwise the caret could be placed only by leaving the box and coming back.

The older caretRangeFromPoint answers about the run of text it found rather than the whole value, so it is taken only for a single-line phrase and declined rather than guessed at otherwise. Where neither API exists the box is still focused, which is the difference between a box that can be typed into and one that cannot.
Only the pointer handlers are attached: the hook's Enter/Space handling on a box people type into would swallow the first space.

commits.subject: Write down which form of a phrase to use, and why
Preview and warm a phrase by what it reads as, not how it is written

body.text: The editor now hands back the source, and two paths sent it straight to ElevenLabs: the preview that fires the moment a voice is chosen, and the warm-up on save. Both would have read "open curly bracket, quote, right, quote" aloud, and stored the clip under text nothing asks for again — so the phrase falls back to the device voice, having been paid for twice.
The test that found the second path failed unmutated, which is how the preview turned up at all.

commits.subject: Open the editor on what a phrase was written as

body.text: The editor opened on phrase.text, which has had its slots resolved into labels. A fill-in-the-blank phrase showed "I want the red/blue one", and saving stored exactly that — flattening the slot for good, with nothing said about it. Long-standing, and destructive.

Phrase now carries its source. It cannot be reconstructed from the display text: "red/blue" is a label, and {pronouns} has become words that would no longer follow the alias table or the user's details.
Voice warming still uses the composed form, so assigning a voice does not fetch a clip of somebody reading brackets aloud.
Also names the actual remedy when a link will not open: allowing pop-ups is the one thing that makes dwelling work.

commits.subject: Say in the guide what a link phrase does when chosen
Open a phrase that is a link, rather than speaking its label

body.text: A phrase whose whole content is a link is a button for going somewhere; saying "cafe.example" out loud is no use to anybody. Choosing one opens it in a new tab and speaks nothing.
The line is drawn at "the link is the whole phrase". A sentence with a link in it still speaks — losing a sentence somebody built to a browser tab is a worse failure than the one this fixes.
A new tab rather than this one, always: the board is how somebody is talking, and navigating it away mid-conversation takes their voice.

commits.subject: Tell a drop from a paste in the tests, and say so in the guide

body.text: With the caret left at the end — which is where typing leaves it — a drop landing at the end and a drop landing at the caret look the same, so the pair of tests covering it proved nothing. Both now move the caret first, one in each direction.

commits.subject: Add a link by pasting or dropping one

body.text: A URL is the worst thing an AAC board can hold as text: long, wrapping a whole row, and forty seconds of punctuation read aloud. Pasting or dropping one now writes [label](url) — the board and the synthesiser see the label, and the address is still there to be copied out.

The label comes from the best thing on offer: the text of a dragged link, then the page title a dragged tab carries, then the site's own name. The URL rides in Style rather than in the text, so everything that reads a phrase's words gets the label without knowing links exist.

A link is drawn, not built. The cell around it is a dwell button whose job is to speak, and a real anchor inside would give a gaze user two targets in one place — the one they did not mean taking the board away mid-sentence.
Only http, https and mailto are accepted. Nothing renders a real anchor today, but this text is copied to a clipboard and a board is a file people hand to each other.

commits.subject: Cover the underscore guard that was not being exercised

body.text: A phrase with underscores only inside words exercises the closing guard alone: with nothing able to close, nothing opens either way. It takes a closing run that is between words to show that an opening one inside a word was refused.

commits.subject: Empty the blank, and let underscores emphasise

body.text: BLANK is now '', so a blank puts no characters into what gets said, copied or typed over — the gap is the placeholder. Two things carry it instead: the drawn underline keeps a minimum width on the board, and composeWithBlank reports where the gap landed so the caret can be put there. Both are needed, because a blank nobody can see is a blank nobody fills.

Searching text for a blank is no longer possible — an empty string matches everywhere — which quietly emptied three tests and would have put the caret at the start of every phrase inserted. hasBlank asks the segments instead.
Underscores now emphasise, with the intraword rule every markdown supporting both delimiters settles on, so snake_case survives.

commits.subject: Make three of the markdown tests actually test something

body.text: Mutation testing found three that passed with the behaviour reverted.
The empty-pair guard was probed with `****`, which never reaches it — the three-asterisk branch is tried first and fails on its own. `~~~~` and a bare pair of backticks do reach it.
The line-start rule was probed with a single-piece line, where the first piece and every piece are the same thing. It needs a slot ahead of the hyphen to say anything.

The audio-cache test picked a voice and saved without touching the text, and picking a voice previews the phrase through `speak`, which already strips — so it passed whether or not `warmVoice` stripped at all. The wording now changes after the voice is chosen, which is the only route that reaches the network through `warmVoice` alone.

commits.subject: Let a phrase carry markdown, and never say it out loud

body.text: A phrase can now be written with emphasis, headings and bullets, so a button can be read at a glance rather than only word by word.

The rule everything follows from is that what the eye sees is styled and what the ear hears is the words. `stripMarkdown` and `layout` walk the same parse and a test holds them to agreeing, because the two coming apart is how a phrase becomes unfindable or gets spoken wrong.

Stripping happens once, inside `speak()` — every route to the synthesiser can arrive with asterisks in hand, since the message box keeps them on purpose. `warmVoice` and the cache warm-up strip the same way, or a clip is stored under text nothing ever asks for again.
Emphasis is asterisks only: `___` is the placeholder for an empty slot, and a parser that ate underscores would swallow it.

commits.subject: Say what the arrows do, and give them room on a phone

body.text: The reorder control is filled while it is on, the way the category tools are — the mode is the loud part, and the two bars should not say it in different voices.
Two fixed-width tools plus six phrases is a lot of bar on a narrow screen, so at 700px the tools give back half their width; they are icons, and it is the phrases that need the room.

commits.subject: Let the emergency bar be arranged

body.text: The bar is the one surface somebody reaches for without reading it, so which button sits where matters more here than anywhere else — and until now the order was whatever Peri shipped.

It now reorders exactly as the category tabs do: drag with a mouse, or hold one button and dwell where it should go. Both routes came from the filter bar, so the state machine behind them moves to `ui/reorder` and both surfaces use it rather than keeping two copies to drift apart.
The arrangement is stored by phrase id, so rewording a phrase leaves it where it was put, and it travels in a backup with the Emergency category.

commits.subject: Start a new phrase from the last category and voice used

body.text: Filing phrases happens in runs — several into one category, several in one voice — and every new one started from the alphabetically first category and from no voice, so the same choice was made over and over.

It is only ever a starting point. A phrase that already has a category or a voice shows its own, so opening one to fix a typo cannot quietly refile it or change how it sounds. That distinction is the whole safety of it, and it has a test in each direction.

Two things that would otherwise seed a phrase with something that no longer exists: a remembered category can be renamed or emptied away, so one that is not in the list is ignored; and unlinking an account takes its voices with it, so a remembered voice from that account is forgotten at the same time.
Kept under its own key and out of backups. It is where somebody had got to, not anything they made.
Eight mutations, all caught. One survived the first pass — nothing checked what happens to a remembered category that has since been deleted, which is the case where a select shows nothing at all.

commits.subject: Turn three either-or phrases into proper choices

body.text: "I'll let her/him know that you called" read the slash out loud. They are now slots — {['her', 'him']} — so the cell offers the two and the message carries only the one that was picked.

Worth knowing when doing this again: a phrase's id hashes its source text, so rewording one in the table gives it a new id. Anyone who had edited, hidden or given a voice to one of these three loses that against the old id, which now names nothing and is skipped. Three phrases is a fair price for phrases that no longer say "slash" out loud; a hundred would not be.

commits.subject: One voice picker, and a chip row that scrolls

body.text: The phrase editor chose a voice through a dropdown while Settings used a full-screen grid, which meant the harder choice — one voice out of sixty, for one phrase — was the one made through the worse control. There is now one `VoicePicker` and both use it. In the editor each voice you try says the phrase itself rather than a sample, because what matters there is how that sentence sounds in that voice.

The filter chips could only be scrolled by a wheel, which is the one thing this app's users do not have. They now sit in a `ScrollRow` with its own dwell arrows, shown only when the row is actually wider than the screen. Two arrows rather than the four a vertical pane gets: this is a handful of chips and the modal's header is busy enough.

`voice/` moves above `ui/` in the layering. The picker is built out of `ui` controls, and the structure test forbids importing sideways, so the two could not stay on the same line. It is also the truer order — `ui` is the more primitive of them.

Found while wiring it: previewing a voice and then assigning it asked for the same clip twice, because the cache cannot dedupe a request that has not come back yet. `synthesize` now hands the second caller the first one's promise, so it is fetched — and billed — once.

Eleven mutations, all caught. Four survived the first pass: three because jsdom lays nothing out, so the arrows never appeared for any test to miss, and one because nothing reopened the editor to see which voice it showed.

commits.subject: Per-phrase voices, voice filters, and audio kept between sessions

body.text: Four things, and the last one is why the other three hang together.

**Filtering a long list.** Sixty device voices plus an account's worth is more than one grid usefully shows. A row of chips above it narrows by collection for the account's voices and by language for the device's — the two kinds divide on different things and a voice only ever belongs to one of them, so one row serves both. "en-GB" is shown as the browser's own name for it.
**A voice per phrase.** The phrase editor gains a Voice setting, off by default. It beats the one in settings wherever that phrase is spoken, and travels in a backup like every other customization.

**Audio that survives a reload.** The cache was memory only, so "assign a voice" would have meant "assign a voice until you close the tab". It is now two layers: memory, which answers synchronously, and IndexedDB, which exists so memory can be full again at start-up. `useBoard` pulls the assigned phrases back in when it mounts. Where IndexedDB is missing — an old browser, a private window, jsdom — everything works and simply forgets between sessions.

**The emergency bar keeps a phrase's voice.** This reverses a rule I wrote and documented, so it is worth being exact about what changed. It used to force the device voice. It now forces *not waiting*, which is what the rule was always for: a phrase whose audio is in hand is said in its own voice, and anything else is said by the device this instant rather than in the right voice a second and a half later. Assigning a voice fetches the audio, so the in-hand case is the ordinary one — and the fallback is unchanged, so a cold cache, a flat connection, or a browser refusing to autoplay all still end in the words being said.

Fifteen mutations, all caught. Three survived the first pass: two because the fixture had no account voice carrying a language and no device voice that could fall into "Other", so neither guard against mixing the two kinds could show; and one because nothing checked that the emergency bar actually passes the phrase's voice, only that speak() honours it when given — the same gap the `local` flag had.
Also clears the audio cache between tests. It is module state, so a clip fetched by one test was answering the next one's request without a fetch.

commits.subject: Confirm signing out, and let the settings panels scroll

body.text: Sign out sat in the same list as Settings and Help, one dwell from any of them, and did it immediately. It now asks first.

The confirmation is a dialog in the middle of the screen rather than a second state on the nav item, because a pointer rests where it last fired — a "yes" appearing under it would be answered by the pointer already sitting there. It is portalled out of the panel for the same reason the pickers are: a panel animated with `transform` makes `position: fixed` resolve against the panel.

It also says what signing out does not do. Somebody whose board is how they speak has every reason to think a button called Sign out might take it away, and it does not — the phrases, the details and the settings all stay.

My details and Settings both grow with what is in them, the first with every contact added and the second with the linked-account row, and neither could be scrolled. Both are now bounded and dwell-scrollable, the same as the guide and the backup screen, so all four menu screens behave the same way. The 68ch column moved inside the scrolling pane so the arrows span the panel rather than the column, which is where the other two put them.
Nothing was testing sign-out at all before this.
Eight mutations, all caught.

commits.subject: Centre the settings panels, and pick backup categories in a grid

body.text: Settings and My details ran the full width of the panel, which on a wide monitor put a setting's label at one edge and its control at the other. They now hold the same 68ch column the guide and the backup screen already used, so the four line up as you move between them.

The backup category list was a stack of full-width rows inside a pane that already scrolls — every category the user has, above the buttons that act on them. It is now a grid behind a trigger, like the voice picker: Everything spanning the top, the categories below it, as many ticked as you like. Cancel puts back what you arrived with, which is what makes trying a selection free.

`PickerModal` and `PickerTile` come out of the voice picker into ui/controls.tsx on the way, since this is the second caller. Both carry the portal that keeps a full-screen modal out of a panel animated with `transform` — without it `position: fixed` resolves against the panel and the grid comes out a few hundred pixels wide.

The tiles now carry a mark as well as the colour when chosen. Green is this app's "selected" cue everywhere, and in a grid where several can be on at once it is a poor thing to read a whole screen by. The old row list had one; the first draft of the grid lost it.
Eight mutations, all caught.

commits.subject: Exercise the windowing inside one category, not the whole table

body.text: Eight tests each mounting all 2,452 cells is more memory than the coverage is worth, and the build machine has less of it than this laptop does.

commits.subject: Stop the grid tests' height stub leaking into every test after them

body.text: Object.defineProperty on HTMLElement.prototype outlives the test that set it, so every element in every later test in the file reported a height of 72px. Benign today — the column count is restored, so the grid still renders everything — but it is the kind of thing that makes a later failure impossible to place.

commits.subject: Render only part of the phrase grid

body.text: Switching back to All rebuilt all 2,452 cells: ~95ms of React reconciliation before the browser is asked to lay any of it out. It now renders a few screens' worth and grows, and the same switch costs ~12ms.

The window grows from the top and is never repositioned by arithmetic. Rows are not a uniform height — a phrase long enough to wrap three times makes its whole row taller, and about one row in five does — so a virtualiser that multiplied a row height by an index would put the grid in the wrong place a fifth of the time. Rendering the first n in normal flow cannot.
Two properties make that safe, and both are mutation-tested:

items: Unmeasured means all of them. Before the first paint, and under jsdom, there is no viewport to measure and the grid renders everything — which is what it did before any of this. That is why the other four hundred tests needed no changes at all.

It cannot strand a phrase. `needsMore` asks for more within a screen's height of the bottom, and content shorter than the viewport is always within a screen of its own end — so a window too small keeps growing until the grid is scrollable, however far off the measurement was.

body.text: Two things found on the way:

items: `performance.now()` is faked by `vi.useFakeTimers()`. My first measurement of this read it and reported 50ms a keystroke, which was the fake clock reporting back the `advanceTimersByTime(50)` I had just given it. Typing was never the slow path — it narrows the grid, so few cells render. Filter changes were, and are what this fixes.
`needsMore` had a redundant line: content shorter than the viewport was already covered by the margin below it. Mutation testing found it by changing it and nothing failing.

body.text: `content-visibility: auto` was already on the cells and stays; it skips layout and paint for what is off screen, which is the browser's half of the same problem. This is the half where React creates two and a half thousand elements.
Ten mutations, all caught. Two of them hang rather than fail — unbounded growth is what happens without the guard that stops it.

commits.subject: Add the profane acronyms, cut to a letter

body.text: 37 more — WTF, STFU, LMAO, FFS, IDGAF, GTFO and the rest — with each profane word cut down to its first letter: "What the f", "Laughing my a off", "Shut the f up".
Adults swear, and a board that cannot puts its user in a register they did not choose. Leaving them out was a decision I should not have made on somebody else's behalf.

Cutting to the first letter rather than to a row of asterisks turns out to be the load-bearing part: the letter left behind is the letter the acronym uses, so every one of them stays findable the way the rest of the category is. "wtf" reaches "What the f", "lmao" reaches "Laughing my a off", "idgaf" reaches "I don't give a f". Thirty-six of the thirty-seven; FU is f-y by initials rather than f-u, and is reached by typing the words.
WTH is in the set without being censored. "Hell" is ordinary speech, and cutting it would be prim rather than careful.

`CENSORED` in the test holds the rule from the positive side — every one of them must still carry a lone letter where a word was taken out — so the check needs no list of the words themselves, and a rewording that spells one back out fails.
Four mutations, all caught.

commits.subject: Add a Texting category of acronym expansions

body.text: 236 of them, from BRB and TTYL through IMO, ICYMI and WFH to GP and A&E.

They are written out in full — "Be right back", not "BRB" — because everything in this app is something somebody might say out loud, and a synthesiser reads BRB as three letters. Typing the acronym still finds most of them: the grid already ranks by initials as well as by prefix, so "ttyl" narrows to "Talk to you later". 165 of the 236 are reachable that way; the rest are found the way any phrase here is, by typing a word in it.

The table records only the expansion, so `core/texting.test.ts` is the one place the pairing is written down, and it holds the category to it from both ends: an expansion that goes missing fails, and a phrase in the category that no acronym asked for fails too. It also checks the expansions read as speech — no placeholder syntax, short enough to text, and starting capitalised.

Nothing profane is in it. Several of the most-used acronyms expand to something this app should not be putting in front of a stranger's carer by default, and a sanitised expansion would be pretending, so they are simply absent. Anyone who wants them can add them in edit mode.

`search` moved from `talk/talk.tsx` to `core/search.ts` on the way. It is pure logic over phrases with no React in it, and the ranking is worth being able to test without rendering two thousand cells — which is what the acronym check does.

Six mutations, all caught. One survived the first pass because it patched a "Talk to you later" in another category: Texting is appended at the end of the table, so the first match in the file is never the one meant.

commits.subject: Top and bottom jumps on every dwell-scrollable pane

body.text: Sixty voices at eighty pixels a dwell is not a way to get through a list, and the voice picker had only the two nudges. It now has the same four controls the phrase grid's rail already offers: jump to the top, nudge up, nudge down, jump to the bottom.

They went into `ScrollPane` rather than into the picker, so the guide, the backup screen and the sign-in page get them too — every one of those is a pane long enough to need scrolling, which is the only condition under which any of these appear at all.

The jump and the nudge share a bar rather than stacking, because two full-width bars top and bottom would cost 56px of a pane that is already height-capped, and splitting each bar in two costs nothing. The jumps carry a double-headed glyph so the pair are told apart without reading the label, and they fire once however long the pointer stays — a jump has nowhere further to go — while the nudges keep repeating while held.
Nine mutations, all caught. Two survived the first pass, both because the test held one nudge and not the other.

commits.subject: Take the voice picker out of the panel that was squashing it

body.text: The picker rendered where it sits in the tree — inside the settings panel. The menu panel is animated with `transform`, and a transformed ancestor makes `position: fixed` resolve against that ancestor rather than the viewport, so `inset: 0` filled the panel instead of the screen. A full-screen grid came out a few hundred pixels wide, squeezed inside the menu it opened from.
It is portalled to the body instead.

Nothing in jsdom lays anything out, so no test could have seen the size. What a test can see is where it sits in the tree, and that is what the new one checks: the picker is not inside `.top-panel`, and its scrim is a child of the body. Both mutations of that are caught.
