The existing picker tests were querying the render container, so the portal put the modal out of their reach and twelve of them failed at once — which is the same fact from the other end, and the reason they now query the document.

commits.subject: Speak each voice as it is chosen

body.text: Nobody can tell sixty voices apart by name. A preview button beside each tile would have put two targets in every one of them, which is the worst thing to give somebody aiming by gaze — so the tile is the preview.

Choosing a voice now speaks a sample in it and leaves the grid open, which turns the picker into the loop it always wanted to be: try one, try the next, keep the one that sounds right. Done keeps the last, Cancel puts back the voice the picker opened on. That revert is what makes trying them free; without it every preview would be a commitment.

The sample is spoken with the voice just picked rather than the one in settings, which has not reached this render yet — and at the volume and speed the app is set to, so it sounds like the thing it is previewing. On a linked account the first try of a voice costs a request; the cache makes every one after it free.
Eight mutations, all caught.

commits.subject: Back on the menu, an inert scrim, and a voice grid

body.text: **Back is on the menu too.** It was on the four panels and not on the menu they open from, on the reasoning that the menu closes rather than goes back. With the scrim no longer a way out that left the menu itself with no exit but the keyboard. It is now in the same corner on all five screens, and from the menu it goes back to the phrases.

**The scrim is inert.** Moving across it used to close the panel after 600ms, so a pointer wandering on its way to the menu took the menu away again — and a gaze user has no way to move without pointing at something. It still swallows pointer events, which is the whole of its remaining job: a phrase behind it must not answer to a dwell that lands on it. Escape still closes, being neither a click nor a dwell.

**Choosing a voice takes the screen.** It was a dropdown in a 186px column inside the panel: sixty device voices in a list two lines high, scrolled by arrows the width of a fingernail. It is now a grid of tiles in a modal, in the same shape the slot picker already uses for the same reason — sixty targets is the one list in this app that genuinely needs the room. The account's voices still lead it, and now say ElevenLabs in the mark's own gold rather than only in the name.

Twenty-one tests, thirteen mutations, all caught. Two survived the first pass and both were my tests being vacuous rather than the code being wrong: `getComputedStyle` proves nothing about a stylesheet jsdom never loaded, so the scrim's rule is read from the file; and the ordering test had no device voices to order the account's against.
Also fixes a shared fixture: `voices` in test/setup.ts was never reset between tests, so the first test to seed one leaked it into every test after.

commits.subject: Organize src into layered directories, and enforce the layering

body.text: Thirty-two files sat flat in src/ under a layering that was documented and nothing more. This makes the layering the directory structure, and then makes a test of it — an import added the wrong way round compiles, passes every other test, and is noticed only when somebody later cannot work out where to put something.

core/                     what Peri knows and keeps. No React, no network ui/  voice/               the shared controls; making sound come out menu/                     the panel that slides down talk/  signin/  legal/    the three screens (root)                    App, main, and the tests that drive the whole app

A directory may import from itself and from anything on an earlier line, never from a later one. src/structure.test.ts checks every import against that, and also the two ways the arrangement quietly rots: a module dropped at the root, where it would sit above everything and answer to no rule at all, and Tailwind widening its scan.
Three things the move turned up, none of which were visible while the files were flat:

items: core/ and voice/ imported each other. store.ts took the account type from elevenlabs.ts while speech.ts took the store — no runtime cycle, since the first is type-only, but neither directory could be read first. An account is something Peri keeps, so its shape now lives with the other kept shapes and voice/ points at core/ one way.
categories.test.tsx was in talk/ but renders <App />. It is a whole-app test, so it belongs at the root beside the other one. The layering test is what noticed.

Tailwind was scanning the whole project for words that look like utility names and finding them in prose. `container.querySelector`, written in AGENTS.md, was shipping a real .container rule with five media queries to every user; words in the stylesheet's own property values added ten more utilities nothing uses. It now gets an allowlist — components, not their tests — which took three kilobytes off the CSS. opacity-30, the one Tailwind class this app actually uses, is the one that survives.

body.text: menu.tsx also gives up the help guide to help-panel.tsx, now that help.ts sits beside it.
Behaviour is unchanged: the 361 tests that existed are untouched and pass, and every rule dropped from the stylesheet is a utility class nothing referenced.

commits.subject: Keep every sent message in a Sent tab

body.text: A conversation repeats itself, and rebuilding a sentence word by word is the slowest thing this app asks of anyone. Everything spoken or copied is now kept, newest first, under a Sent tab pinned to the left of All. Resting on one puts it back in the message box, ready to go again in a single dwell.

Three things count as sending, because all three are the message leaving: pressing Speak, copying to the clipboard, and — in auto-speak, where the phrase never reaches the box at all — choosing a phrase. Copying is recorded only once the clipboard confirms it took it.

Saying the same thing twice moves it back to the top rather than listing it again: the list is for reaching a sentence quickly, and ten copies of "yes please" makes that harder. The last two hundred are kept.

Sent is not a category. Its filter id starts with a space, which no real one can ever match — names are trimmed before they are saved — and both it and All now carry `fixed: true`, which is how FilterBar knows a tab cannot be renamed, dragged or reordered. That replaces the hard-coded check for "all" it had before.

In edit mode a sent message is not editable, because there is nothing in it to edit: the dialog offers Keep, which files it as a phrase of the user's own in a category they choose, and Forget, which takes it off the list. Somebody who has just said something private needs the second one.

The list is never in a backup. It is a record of what somebody actually said — what hurts, what they want, who they were asking for — and a backup is a file made to be handed to somebody else. Its own storage key, outside the three things buildBackup reads, with a test holding it there.

Seventeen mutations, all caught. Two of them survived the first pass — the cap and the empty-message guard are unreachable from the UI, since the buttons that would trigger them are disabled, so they now have unit tests of their own.

commits.subject: Link an ElevenLabs account and use its voices

body.text: Settings gains an ElevenLabs row. Paste the API key and its voices join the same picker as the device ones, above them — someone who went to the trouble of linking an account is looking for those, not scrolling past sixty the browser came with.
The device voice is instant, free and works offline. These are none of those things, and that difference shapes everything here.

**A phrase never fails into silence.** A flat connection, an expired key, a rate limit, a browser refusing to autoplay without a recent click — every one of them ends in the device speaking the words instead. That last one is not an edge case for this app: a dwell is a timer, not a click, and Chrome blocks audio started from one.
**The emergency bar always speaks on the device**, whatever is selected. A request going out and coming back is not what "I can't breathe" needs, and with the network down it is nothing at all.

**Audio is kept once fetched.** An AAC board is the same couple of thousand phrases said over and over, so the second time costs nothing and arrives instantly. Bounded at two hundred so a day of talking cannot grow it without limit.

**The key never enters a backup.** It lives under its own storage key, outside the three things buildBackup is built from, and a test holds it there — a backup is made to be shared, and the key in one hands over the account along with whatever it can be billed for.

Sending the words to a third party is a disclosure, so the privacy policy said the wrong thing until now: it promised they never leave the device and that the app makes no requests once cached. Both are corrected, the guide gains a "Better voices" section saying the same, and the settings row says it at the point of linking. The three have to agree.
Also promotes BackupButton to ui.tsx as PanelButton — this is its third caller, and a fourth copy of the same dwell button was not worth writing.

commits.subject: Put Back in the top right of every panel

body.text: It used to sit under the panel's content, which meant it moved with it: the settings panel, your details, the backup screen and the guide are all different heights, so the way out was somewhere different on each of them, and somewhere different again once a panel's own content changed. A target that has to be found again each time is a poor one for anybody aiming by gaze.

It now sits in the row that was already at the top of the panel, at the right hand end of it, so it is in the same place on all four — and above the content rather than below, so nothing the content does can move it.
The user's name gives up its width rather than pushing Back off the edge when an email is long.

Ten tests, four of them run against each panel in turn: that Back is the last thing in the top row, that it goes back, that the menu itself does not offer one — it closes rather than goes back — and that it answers a dwell, a tap and a key like every other control. Five mutations, all caught.

commits.subject: Close the three gaps the refactor turned up

body.text: Mutation-testing the refactored code found three behaviours that no test guarded — all of them with a comment in the source explaining why they matter, which is how they were spotted.

items: The caret lands on a phrase's blank, selected, ready to type over. A dwell user cannot place a caret by clicking, so this is the whole of that feature.
Deleting the last phrase in a category takes its tab away, and the filter falls back to All. Without it the grid sat empty under a tab that no longer existed, with no way back to it.
The scroll rail scrolls the grid it sits beside. It is the only way down two thousand phrases for anyone without a wheel or a scrollbar.

body.text: Five mutations of those paths, all caught.
Also documents the new layout: which file owns what, that imports only point down the list, and why the stylesheet stays one file.

commits.subject: Un-export two internals the refactor left visible
Extract the talking screen's state into three hooks

body.text: TalkScreen was 580 lines with thirteen pieces of state and twenty callbacks threaded between them. Splitting the file did not touch that; this does.
use-board.ts     what is on the board and every way of changing it use-composer.ts  the message, its history, and the caret use-toast.ts     the line that appears and fades

What is left in talk.tsx is the screen's own business: which dialog is open, which category is showing, whether the app is in edit mode or resting, and what to say when an operation finishes. The board reports what it did and the screen decides whether to announce it, so the same operation can stay silent where the screen already shows the result.

Two components came out with it: Topbar, which owns the message box and the dwell that focuses it, and PhraseGrid, which owns the reference between the grid and the rail that scrolls it — nobody else's business.
Two things the tests could not have caught, found by reading:

items: `copy()` with an empty message resolved as a success and would have flashed "Copied to clipboard" over nothing. The button is disabled there, so it was unreachable — but the guard belongs in the screen, which is where the message lives, so that is where it went.

`deliverPhrase` briefly depended on the whole composer object, which is a fresh object every render. It feeds the memoised phrase cells, so that would have re-rendered all two thousand of them on every unrelated render. It depends on `insert` again, as it did before.

commits.subject: Split App.tsx into modules along the seams it already had

body.text: App.tsx was 2,935 lines and held every screen, every control and every dialog. The section banners inside it were already the seams; this makes them files.
Nothing changed but where the code lives. The 279 tests are untouched and pass, and the built stylesheet is byte-identical to the one before the split.
The layering, leaves first:

style.ts, settings.ts, edit-mode.ts, icons.tsx   no dependants of their own ui.tsx                                           the controls every screen shares grid, slots, filter-bar, emergency, editors,     one surface each topbar, settings-panel, profile-panel, backup-panel menu.tsx                                         hosts the four panels talk.tsx, signin.tsx, legal-page.tsx             the three screens App.tsx                                          which screen is on
Three things moved to where they belonged rather than to a file of their own:

items: Arranging categories is store manipulation — renameCategory takes a store and returns a patch for one — so it went to store.ts.
The emergency phrases are phrase data built with plainPhrase, so they went to phrases.ts.
cx and dwellVar are not components, and a module mixing the two loses fast refresh for every screen importing one, so they went to style.ts.

body.text: The contexts are their own modules because ui.tsx needs a dwell time and would otherwise have to import the settings screen — which is built out of ui.tsx.

commits.subject: Leave an untouched profile out of a backup

body.text: Writing a name of three empty strings meant the panel offered someone "your details" when they had entered none — and replacing from that file would have quietly cleared the name on the device receiving it.

commits.subject: Add backup, restore and sharing

body.text: Everything a user has made of Peri lives in this browser and nowhere else. Clearing site data, a new tablet, or a switch of browser takes all of it, and for someone whose board is how they speak that is not a small loss. There was no way out and no way in.
Menu → Backup & sharing saves it as one file, or brings one back. Ticking categories instead of Everything narrows the file to those, which is also how a set of phrases gets handed to somebody else.

A backup is a diff against the phrase table, not a copy of it. The table ships with the app, so the file holds what the user did — added, reworded, moved, removed, rearranged — plus their details and settings. Ids hash the source text, so one still names the same phrase in a later release, and one that names nothing is skipped rather than restored as a ghost.
Two decisions worth stating:

items: Merging never takes a phrase away. Deleting is the one change the app offers no way back from, so a file someone else made does not get to make one on your device. Only replacing applies removals, and it is refused for a file covering a few categories — everything it said nothing about would go.

Imported settings are held to the same limits as the settings panel. A dwell time of zero fires every control the instant a pointer crosses it, which for a gaze user leaves no working control to undo it with.

body.text: The file picker is a real <input> filling the button rather than a dwell handler that clicks a hidden one: the browser opens it only for a genuine click or an Enter on the input, never for a timer. Paste is the way in for anyone whose dwell never produces a click at all.

src/store.ts is new and holds what App.tsx used to: the persisted shapes and their four localStorage keys. The backup format has to be written against the same definitions the app runs on — a second copy would drift, and an export that no longer matches the store is a backup that silently restores nothing.

commits.subject: Fix the placeholders the edits left malformed

body.text: 41 phrases. Most are mechanical: `{{'great', 'awful']}` for `{[…]}`, a `{[…]` with no closing brace, a missing opening quote, and rows of dots that became `{}..` or `{}.?` or `{}{}`.

The existing invariants already caught ten of these, because they leaked a brace into what the cell renders. The rest were silent — a list quietly one option short, two blanks asking the same question twice. Three tests are added for that class, since it is the kind that ships.

`{utensil}` is left as written. `lookupAlias` already tries a name, its plural and its singular, so it finds the `utensils` list — which is also why phrases have always said `{direction}` against a `directions` list. Normalising them would have been churn against the table's own convention.
Applied to the JSON as text rather than by reparsing it, so the file keeps its own formatting and the diff is only the lines that changed.

commits.subject: Phrase table edits

body.text: Spero's edits, committed as received so the fixes that follow are reviewable against them:

items: New alias groups `utensils` and `meals`, which several phrases already referenced without them existing.
Ellipses turned into `{}` blanks, so the cursor lands in them for typing rather than leaving a row of dots to be overtyped.
Parenthetical alternatives — "It was so good (bad)" — turned into pickers.
Spacing normalised inside placeholder braces.

commits.subject: Give shared links a preview image

body.text: A link to Peri is most likely to be shared with someone who needs it, by someone explaining what it is. Without an og:image that arrives as a blank card, which is a poor introduction to a communication aid.
The 512px icon does the job. Root-relative rather than absolute so it survives deploy previews and a change of domain; every current scraper resolves it.
The test checks the file is actually there, since a preview image that 404s looks exactly like no preview image at all.

commits.subject: Let the site be indexed

body.text: The noindex was a Figma Make default that came with the scaffold, not a decision anyone made. Peri is a free communication aid; someone looking for one should be able to find it rather than needing to be sent a link.

robots.txt now allows everything and the robots meta tag is gone. The file is kept rather than deleted — a missing robots.txt is a 404 on every crawl, and an explicit one states the intent where the next person will look.
The two still have to agree, and the test that enforces that gains a second check: an empty or missing robots.txt agrees with anything, so the first check would have passed while every crawl failed.

commits.subject: Remove Figma Make

body.text: The project was scaffolded by Figma Make and has not needed it for a while. What it was still doing:

items: .figma/make/ — seven shell scripts, each a one-line wrapper over a pnpm script, plus two config files.
Four Vite plugins in vite.config.ts, three of them dev-only aids for the Figma preview iframe. The fourth assembled index.html at build time from .figma/make/site.json.

body.text: That last one is why index.html held `<!-- figma:title -->` rather than a title: the plugin filled the slots. Those are now written out plainly, which also settles the one thing the rename could not reach — the browser tab said DwellSpeak because nothing in this repo controlled it.
vitest.config.ts is folded back into vite.config.ts. It was only ever separate because Figma Make regenerated that file and would have overwritten anything put in it.
Two things the plugin was doing that had to be preserved rather than dropped:

items: robots.txt, generated on every build from `robots.index: false`. It is now a static file. Removing it silently would have made the site indexable for the first time — a change to how it appears in the world, not a build detail, and not one to make as a side effect of deleting a build tool.
The description and og: tags, which came from the same config and are now written in index.html.

body.text: src/shell.test.ts is new: index.html and the manifest are the parts of the app no component renders, so nothing else here would notice them breaking. It checks the title is real rather than an unfilled slot, that every file they reference exists, and that robots.txt and the robots meta tag still agree.

commits.subject: Rename the app to Peri and build its icons from the new mark

body.text: The name changes wherever a person reads it: the sign-in page, the help guide, the privacy policy and terms, the menu, the manifest, and the iOS home-screen title.

The storage keys deliberately do not change. All four still say `dwellspeak_`, and everything a user has — their phrases, their edits, their dwell times — lives under them and nowhere else. Renaming without a migration would silently empty the app for everyone already using it. The name is cosmetic; the data is not.
Icons come from the supplied mark. Two things the old set got wrong are fixed along the way:

items: apple-touch-icon pointed at an SVG, which iOS ignores — so an installed copy had no home-screen icon at all. It is now a 180px PNG, full-bleed and unrounded, since iOS applies its own mask.
The manifest offered SVG only. PNGs at 192 and 512 are listed alongside for the platforms that still want them.

body.text: The maskable icon keeps the mark well inside the safe zone so an adaptive mask cannot clip it.

The service worker cache is renamed with it, which doubles as the generation bump the new artwork needs: assets are served cache-first, so an installed copy would otherwise keep the old mark indefinitely.

commits.subject: Shrink Rest to a lozenge on the message box

body.text: 44px of reserved grid height was too much to spend on it. It is now 8rem by 0.5rem, straddling the top edge of the message box — the middle of the screen's top, where a gaze on its way anywhere passes — and costs the grid nothing.

No icon and no word fit at that height, so the name lives in aria-label alone and the state is told by the whole app dimming behind it. The dwell fill runs the lozenge's full height rather than a 3px strip, which at 8px would have been most of the control anyway.

Half a rem is well under the 24px a pointing device wants, and this app is driven by head and eye trackers, so the area that answers to a pointer is 20px tall and invisible. The painted size is the one that was asked for.

commits.subject: Add a Rest button that switches dwell off everywhere but itself

body.text: Dwell is this app's only input, which means there has been no way to look at the screen without choosing something. A gaze that wanders while its owner reads, thinks, or simply rests has been firing phrases the whole time.
Rest switches every control off at once. It is the only one that stays live — it has to be the way back — and it says so by opting out of the resting state its own context provides.

Resting gates the control rather than only its hover path: tap and Enter go through the same check, or resting would only be resting for one of the three ways a control can fire. Any dwell already part-way through is abandoned, since it would otherwise land after rest began, which is the one thing rest is for.

It sits over the phrases, where a wandering gaze is most likely to be when it needs stopping, and the grid area is padded to make room so it never covers a phrase. Amber, because green already means selected and blue means held. While resting the rest of the app dims to 45% — enough to say nothing will answer, not so far that it cannot be read, since reading is most of why someone rests.

Note this puts the emergency phrases behind two dwells rather than one while resting. That is the trade: leaving them live would mean a resting gaze could call 911 by accident, which is the failure that matters more.

commits.subject: Fit the sign-in page on one screen, and make what spills dwell-scrollable

body.text: The page ran to about 1000px with three providers on offer. Anything below that scrolled, and a dwell user has no wheel and no scrollbar — so on a phone the guest button, the sign-in buttons and the dwell-time control were all below the fold and unreachable. The one screen nobody can skip was the one screen they could not use.
Two changes, because either alone is not enough.

The page now gives ground as height runs out, in order of what it can afford to lose: feature blurbs, then the feature list, then everything promotional but the name. It never touches the dwell-time control or the ways in — someone who needs a slow dwell cannot reach anything without the first, and nobody gets past this page without the second.

And the content sits in the same ScrollPane the settings panel uses, so what still does not fit — a phone on its side has barely 400px, and the buttons alone want 400 — gets dwell arrows. The page itself no longer scrolls: the arrows live at the edges of a fixed frame, and would otherwise scroll away with everything else.
That frame also puts `dvh` after `vh` rather than before it, so the fallback stops overriding the value it is a fallback for.

commits.subject: Swap the sort button's icon with its arrangement

body.text: The green fill was the only thing saying which of the two arrangements was on, and neither of them is "off" — so colour was carrying a distinction it should never carry alone. The icon now changes with it: tidy lines descending under an A-to-Z arrow, or the same lines jumbled beside a grip. Neither can be mistaken for the reorder button's opposing arrows, which sits right next to them.
The name follows suit, stating the arrangement before the switch: "Your own order. Switch to A to Z". Naming only the action left it contradicting the fill it sits inside.
Class renamed to sort-order-tab, since it has not been the sort-alphabetically button since it became a toggle.

commits.subject: Make A–Z a toggle rather than a way to lose your order

body.text: Sorting alphabetically threw the custom arrangement away, so someone who wanted a quick look down an alphabetical list had to rebuild theirs a tab at a time to get it back. Nobody would risk pressing it twice.

The arrangement is now kept either way and the same control switches between the two, saying which way it will go: "Sort categories A to Z" or "Use your own category order". It is inert until there is an order of their own to return to.
Rearranging while A–Z is showing still replaces the stored order — that is building a new one, not editing the old — and switches back to showing it.
Stores written before the flag existed have an order and no flag; an order someone took the trouble to make is the one they were looking at, so they load as custom.

commits.subject: Shrink the filter arrows on narrow screens

body.text: Four of them spend 144px before a single category is visible, and on a phone that competes with both the category tools and the tabs themselves. The arrows give way first: they repeat, and the tools do not — being findable is the whole reason those sit outside the scroller.
28px rather than 36px, at the 700px breakpoint the grid already uses. They keep full bar height, which is the dimension a dwell actually needs, and stay clear of the 24px minimum target size.

commits.subject: Move add out of the scroller too

body.text: Leaving it in with the tabs while sorting and reordering moved out split three controls that do the same kind of job across two places. All three now sit past the scroll arrows.

Add and sort share the first slot. Adding a category mid-reorder would drop whatever is in the air, so the two are never offered at once — and sharing the slot keeps the toolbar a constant width, so the reorder button does not shift under the pointer when the mode is toggled.

commits.subject: Park the ordering controls past the scroll arrows

body.text: They sat in with the tabs, at the far end of a bar that can run to dozens of categories — so finding them meant scrolling there first, which is a lot of dwelling for a control you are looking for rather than one you already know is there. They now sit outside the scroller, always in the same place, and a size larger than the pills that scroll past them.
Adding a category stays in with the tabs: it makes one, and categories are what the scroller holds. Ordering is a property of the bar itself.

commits.subject: Move the held-tab reduced-motion rule in with the others

body.text: The file keeps every reduced-motion override in one block, each naming the animation it stops, so a reader looking for what stops moving finds all of it in one place. Making the raised position the rule's own transform rather than a keyframe lets the override be the single line the others are.

commits.subject: Make a held category unmistakable

body.text: The lifted tab was ghosted to 55% opacity, which read as "disabled" — exactly backwards for the one thing in the bar the user is holding. On a tab that small it was easy to miss altogether.
It is now the loudest thing there: filled, bold, ringed like a chip lifted out of a socket, and bobbing slowly. Three further cues, because colour alone cannot carry it:

items: A distinct blue rather than another green pill. "Selected" is already a filled green pill and the two states must never be mistaken. Blue also stays separable from green under the common colour-vision deficiencies.
Every other category takes a dashed outline, so the whole bar changes state and reads from the corner of an eye.
The lift is announced in the live region, which says aloud what no amount of styling can.

body.text: `.filter-scroll` clips its vertical overflow, so the bob is small and the padding there was widened to fit it rather than have it cut off.

commits.subject: Put down a lifted category when reordering is switched off

body.text: Found by mutation testing the previous commit: leaving reorder mode with a tab in the air left it there. Coming back, the next dwell dropped the forgotten tab instead of lifting the one under the pointer.

The guard that was supposed to cover this only masked the held tab while the mode was off, so it came back holding the same one. Clearing it on the toggle is the actual fix, and the derived guard goes — one mechanism rather than two, neither of which worked.

commits.subject: Let categories be ordered alphabetically or by hand

body.text: Categories have always been alphabetical, which is fine until the ones you reach for most sit at the wrong end of a bar you have to dwell your way along. They can now be arranged by hand, and put back.
Reordering is a mode inside edit mode rather than a gesture on the tabs themselves, because those tabs already answer a dwell by opening for rename. Within it a tab can be moved two ways:

items: Lift and drop — one dwell picks a tab up, a second dwell on another drops it there. Pointer-drag needs a button held down while the pointer moves, which is the one gesture a dwell user cannot make, so it cannot be the only way in. Dwelling the lifted tab again puts it back.
Native drag, for a mouse.

body.text: Order is stored as a list of names. Empty means alphabetical, which is both the default and what the A–Z button returns to; a name the list has never heard of sits at the end, so adding a category later does not have to rewrite it. Renames carry the position across and deletes remove it.

commits.subject: Focus the message box by dwell when it is not already focused

body.text: Outside edit mode the box is a typing surface, and reaching it meant clicking — the one input a dwell-only user cannot produce. So the message was theirs to build with the grid but not to correct by hand. Holding on it now moves focus there.

The hold stops arming once the box already holds focus: a pointer left resting there while its owner types should not sit re-arming and flashing a progress bar at them. It arms again as soon as focus moves away.

commits.subject: Correct the comment on the composer key handler

body.text: Mutation testing showed attaching it unconditionally breaks nothing: the hook's own disabled check already returns before cancelling Space. The conditional is still worth keeping — that check reads a ref synced in an effect — but the comment claimed a bug it does not actually prevent.

commits.subject: Make the message box answer to dwell, and carry its text into the editor

body.text: The message box was the only control in the app that could be activated by a click and nothing else, and in edit mode it is the only way to add an ordinary phrase. A dwell-only user — the app's whole audience — could not add one at all. It now behaves like every other control: hover and hold, or Enter/Space for switch access, with the same progress bar.
The dwell is disabled outside edit mode, where the box is for typing, and the key handler is only attached in edit mode because the hook cancels Space to stop the grid scrolling underneath.

Adding from the message box now seeds the editor with whatever is composed there, so a message worth keeping becomes a phrase without retyping it. It is kept off the edit context deliberately: `openEdit` is read by every phrase cell, and making it depend on the message text would re-render the grid on each keystroke.

commits.subject: Make the category-move tests actually test the move

body.text: Mutation testing caught a vacuous test. "Files a phrase under a category invented on the spot" asserted only that the tab appeared — which happens via store.categories whether or not the phrase moved — so it passed with the move deliberately broken.
It now follows through: leave edit mode, select the new category, and check the phrase is in it. Plus a second case moving a phrase between two categories that already exist.
Re-verified: breaking the move now fails both, where before it failed neither.

commits.subject: Let categories be added and renamed in edit mode

body.text: Categories were derived from whatever the phrases happened to say, so there was no way to create one, rename one, or move a phrase between them.

Edit mode now makes the filter tabs editable, matching what it already does to phrase cells: dwell a tab to rename it, or use the + at the end of the bar to add one. Renaming is stored as a source-name mapping rather than per phrase, so one entry renames a whole category including the built-in phrases in it — which per-phrase overrides could not have done.

A category can exist before it holds anything, so one can be made first and filled afterwards. It can only be deleted while empty; deleting a populated one would take its phrases with it silently, so the dialog explains that instead and offers no delete.
Renaming onto a name already in use merges the two, which is the only sane reading of giving two categories the same name.

Fixes a gap this uncovered: the phrase editor has always shown a category selector for existing phrases, but saving discarded it, so changing a phrase's category did nothing at all. Moves are now stored per phrase and take precedence over a category-wide rename.
The phrase editor also gained a "New category…" option, so a phrase can be filed under a category invented while writing it.
14 new tests covering the store shape, the merge and double-rename cases, that a rename carries its phrases, and that a populated category cannot be deleted.

commits.subject: Add a privacy policy and terms of service

body.text: The sign-in page has always said "you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy" while neither document existed — the same shape of false claim as the offline and sync promises fixed earlier, and the last one left. Meta also requires a published privacy policy URL before an app can go Live, so this blocks Facebook sign-in besides.

Both are served at /privacy and /terms as standalone documents. They render with no account and none of the app around them, because the consoles fetch these URLs directly and a visitor may never have signed in. Two leaf pages reached by real links need no router.

The privacy policy describes what the app actually does: no servers, no analytics, no cookies, everything in localStorage on the device. It also discloses the two things that are easy to leave out and untrue to omit — that some operating systems offer cloud voices which send the text to be spoken to their own servers, and that Netlify logs requests like any host.

The terms lead with the emergency warning rather than burying it. The app has a "Call 911" button that only speaks aloud; nobody should be left believing it summons help. It says so plainly and tells people to keep a separate, non-digital way of calling for help.
help.ts and legal.ts now share prose types, and the section renderer is shared between the help panel and the legal pages.

31 new tests. The content tests assert the specific claims — nothing collected, data stays local, cloud voices disclosed, not a medical device, emergency phrases contact nobody — so if the app ever starts collecting something, the tests are what force the policy to change.
Not written by a lawyer. Accurate as to behaviour, but worth review before it is relied on.

commits.subject: Stop the test suite depending on local OAuth config

body.text: Vite loads .env.local during tests, so the sign-in tests asserted "no provider configured" by relying on the developer not having configured any. The moment someone sets VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID to work on sign-in, two tests fail on their machine while staying green on CI — the worst shape for a failure, since the gate cannot see it.
Vitest now pins the three variables to empty. Tests that care about a configured provider stub it themselves, which auth.test.ts already did.
Verified against all three cases: a real .env.local present, all three providers set via the environment, and a clean machine with no .env.local at all. 43 tests pass in each.

commits.subject: Make the OAuth sign-ins actually work

body.text: All three providers were wired to SDKs but had no credentials and two real defects, so none of them could have worked as written.

Google used One Tap via prompt(). That path needs Google's own rendered button and is suppressed outright in browsers without third-party cookies, so a dwell user would have got a button that silently did nothing; its isNotDisplayed/isSkippedMoment callbacks are deprecated besides. Replaced with the OAuth token popup flow, which works from our own button, followed by a userinfo fetch.
Facebook waited on fbAsyncInit every time. That fires once per page load, so a second attempt hung forever with the spinner up and no way back. The SDK is now reused when already present.

The script loader resolved as soon as a tag with the right id existed, so two overlapping attempts could continue with the SDK still undefined. It now caches one promise per script and waits for the real load event.

Providers without a credential are no longer shown at all — a button that can only fail is worse than no button. Guest sign-in is unaffected, so the app is fully usable with nothing configured, which is how it ships.
Closing the popup is now silent rather than an error, since cancelling is a decision.

docs/oauth-setup.md walks through all three consoles, including the parts that catch people out: Apple refusing localhost, Apple sending a name only on the first authorisation ever, Facebook's email permission being optional, and env changes needing a redeploy on Netlify.
The doc also states plainly that this is not authentication — no server verifies anything, so a signed-in user has proven nothing. Building on that assumption would need a backend.
13 new tests. Verified the provider gating bites: showing all three regardless fails 2.

commits.subject: Give the help guide a reading column

body.text: The menu panel spans the full viewport, so on a wide monitor the guide's lines ran the whole width — a measure of a couple of hundred characters, where comfortable reading is 45 to 75. Long lines are hard to track back from the end of one line to the start of the next, which is exactly the wrong tax to put on this audience.
The prose now sits in a centred 68ch column. It fills the panel as before on a phone, where the constraint never binds.
Sizes were also raised — body text from 13px to 14.5px, with more line spacing and more room between sections. 13px suits the control rows around it; long-form reading needs more.

commits.subject: Add a user guide under Menu → Help

body.text: The app explained itself nowhere. Everything about it — that you select by resting rather than clicking, that some phrases hold a word to choose, what the two buttons at the top of the right-hand column do — had to be discovered.

The guide is written for two readers at once: the person using the app and whoever helps them set it up. Short sentences, plain words, no jargon. Someone may be reading it while tired, and every screenful costs them dwell time.
Ten sections cover selecting, building a message, phrases with a choice, auto-speak, the emergency bar, editing, personal details, settings, keyboard and switch access, and offline use.
Kept as data in src/help.ts rather than markup, so it stays readable, stays testable, and can be translated later without touching the component.

The panel needs its own scroll arrows — a dwell user can reach neither a scrollbar nor a wheel — so the voice dropdown's scroller is generalised into ScrollPane and both now share it. Text selection is re-enabled inside the guide, since the app disables it globally.

20 new tests. The content tests assert the guide still names each shipped feature, so a feature added without a mention here fails the build rather than leaving the guide quietly wrong. Verified they bite: removing the Help entry fails 5, and renaming auto-speak in the guide fails 1.

commits.subject: Point code of conduct reports at a named person

body.text: info@auli.tech is the organisation's general inbox, which is the wrong destination for reports that are confidential by nature. spero@auli.tech reaches one person directly.

commits.subject: Add contributing guide

body.text: Documents the conventions this repo has accumulated, weighted toward the ones a newcomer would otherwise learn by tripping over them.

The accessibility section is the important one. Every control must work by dwell, tap and keyboard — not two of the three — because someone driving this with a head tracker, a switch or a keyboard all need to reach the same things. useDwellControl gives all three; hardcoded dwell durations and missing keyboard paths are the failures to watch for.

Also written down: run pnpm check before pushing and why (netlify.toml uses it as the build command, so a failing test fails the deploy); prove a regression test fails without its fix, since one that passes with the bug reintroduced is worse than none; use pnpm rather than npm; and the four things that surprise people — vite.config.ts being regenerated, exhaustive-deps being an error, the tree not being formatter-clean, and slot arity deciding the phrase interaction.
Every command, path and claim in it was checked against the repo rather than written from memory.

commits.subject: Add MIT licence and code of conduct

body.text: The repo had no licence at all, which by default leaves it all rights reserved — nobody could legally use or contribute to it.

LICENSE is MIT, copyright Autonomous Living Technologies, Inc., taken from the GitHub organisation's registered name rather than invented. package.json gains the matching `license` field so tooling agrees with the file.

CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md is Contributor Covenant 2.1, pulled verbatim from upstream rather than retyped, with its front matter stripped and the reporting placeholder replaced by the organisation's published contact.
Verified: the licence body is identical to the SPDX MIT text once whitespace is normalised, and no unfilled placeholder remains in the code of conduct.

commits.subject: Pin pnpm to 11.20.0 everywhere

body.text: .mise.toml declared 10.34.3 while the lockfile had been regenerated by 11.20.0. Same lockfile format, so nothing was broken, but the repo described a toolchain nobody was using.
netlify.toml pins pnpm as well — its comment says it mirrors .mise.toml, which Netlify does not read — so both move together. Leaving one behind would have relocated the drift rather than removed it.
Verified pnpm 11.20.0 installs this lockfile with --frozen-lockfile, the same check run against 10.34.3 before it was pinned.
Only the deploy preview exercises the Netlify side, since the build image resolves PNPM_VERSION itself.

commits.subject: Drop the deprecated baseUrl from tsconfig

body.text: `paths` has resolved relative to the tsconfig file since TypeScript 4.1, so `baseUrl` is redundant here. It is flagged as deprecated in editors, and its remaining behaviour — resolving bare specifiers against the project root — is the part TypeScript is moving away from. The `paths` entry already uses a `./` prefix, so nothing else has to change.
Module resolution is `bundler`, and Vite and Vitest each declare the `@` alias themselves, so this only ever affected typechecking.
Verified by adding a temporary file importing through `@/`: it resolves with baseUrl gone, and a deliberately bogus `@/does-not-exist` still fails with TS2307, so the check was not passing vacuously.

commits.subject: Let users fill the contact and name aliases

body.text: phrasetable.json reserves aliases for `contacts` and `name`, but ships them empty with nowhere to put a particular person's details. Six phrases depended on them and rendered as dead text: "I'm going to call ___", "This is ___".

Adds a profile — nickname, first and last name, and a contact list — edited under Menu → My details and stored in its own localStorage key. Its values overlay the table's empty entries when phrases are parsed, so those phrases come alive as soon as anything is filled in. With nothing filled in, behaviour is exactly as before.
Slot arity now decides the interaction, which matters because a name is a single value rather than a choice:
0 options   ___ , cursor lands on it to type over 1 option    substituted straight in, no picker  ("This is Ada") 2+ options  the slot picker, as before          ("call Mum" / "call Dad")
That is why hasChoices and choosableSlots key off `options.length > 1`.
Phrase ids hash the source text rather than the rendered text, so a profile edit cannot detach a user's saved phrase edits — covered by a test.
Three phrases stay blanks on purpose: "Did you see {}" and friends name no alias, so there is nothing to fill them with.
18 new tests. Verified they bite by reverting the behaviour: ignoring the profile overlay fails 7, and letting a single-value slot open a one-option picker fails 11.

commits.subject: Gate the Netlify deploy on the test suite

body.text: Netlify already builds and publishes each PR, but `vite build` succeeding is not evidence the app works: every defect fixed in this repo's history compiled cleanly and shipped broken. Making the build command run the tests turns the existing Netlify check into a real gate, without adding a second CI system and a second status to interpret.
Also pins the toolchain and fixes the cache headers the PWA work needs:

NODE_VERSION / PNPM_VERSION  mirror .mise.toml, which Netlify does not read. Verified pnpm 10.34.3 installs this lockfile with --frozen-lockfile. sw.js, manifest, index.html  must-revalidate. The service worker decides when clients get new code, so serving it from cache lets an installed PWA pin itself to an old build indefinitely. /assets/*                    immutable; Vite fingerprints them. SPA fallback                 deep links land on the app, not a 404.

Note this file takes precedence over the equivalent Netlify UI settings, which is the point — the deploy becomes reviewable in the repo — but it means any UI-only settings for base directory or functions need folding in here.
Verified: the TOML parses, `pnpm check && pnpm build` passes, and dist still contains the PWA assets.

commits.subject: Add a test suite (Vitest, jsdom, Testing Library)

body.text: Verification for the last three merges ran from throwaway scripts that drove the production bundle. They caught real defects but guarded nothing, and drifted twice when selectors changed under them. This lands that coverage as tests, plus the cases the scripts could not reach.
67 tests in three files:

phrases.test.ts  Placeholder parsing and alias resolution, including the malformed table entries, and whole-table invariants over all 2,185 phrases. dwell.test.tsx   The dwell hook against fake timers — the timing path the bundle scripts never exercised, since they could only click. App.test.tsx     Whole-app flows: sign-in, composing, slot pickers, auto-speak, emergency bar, edit mode, keyboard access.
Several are explicit regression guards for defects fixed earlier in this branch's history, and each was checked by reverting the fix and confirming the test fails:
drop mainPhrases from the visiblePhrases deps -> 2 failures let dwell and click both fire                 -> 1 failure strip brackets the way the original did       -> 13 failures

Config notes: vitest.config.ts is standalone rather than a `test` block in vite.config.ts, which Figma Make regenerates. The app grid renders every phrase, so tests query with querySelector — getByRole builds an accessibility tree over thousands of cells and is slow enough to matter.

Adds `pnpm test`, `pnpm test:watch`, and `pnpm check` (typecheck, lint, test). AGENTS.md documents the layout, the two testing gotchas, and the expectation that a bug fix arrives with a test proven to fail without it.

commits.subject: Clear all Dependabot advisories (vite, postcss)

body.text: Nine open alerts, all against two packages:
vite     5 alerts, needed >= 8.0.16   was 8.0.3   now 8.2.0 postcss  4 alerts, needed >= 8.5.23   was 8.5.8   now 8.5.25
postcss reaches the tree only through vite, so updating vite resolves both. Tailwind and the React plugin came along within their existing semver ranges to keep the toolchain consistent.

Both are dev dependencies — they build the app rather than ship in it, so nothing here reaches a user's browser. Worth patching regardless: the vite advisories cover the dev server, which does listen on 0.0.0.0 in this project's dev script.

pnpm audit now reports zero vulnerabilities at every severity. Typecheck, lint and build are clean, and both headless interaction suites still pass on the new toolchain: phrase insertion, slot pickers, keyboard activation, speech, edit mode, and the auto-speak toggle.

commits.subject: Add auto-speak toggle to the grid rail

body.text: Selecting a phrase always composed it into the message box, which suits building a sentence but is a detour when the phrase *is* the utterance. Auto-speak makes the grid a one-tap talker: the phrase is spoken through the user's voice, volume and rate settings, and the message box is left untouched.

The toggle sits above the edit toggle in the right-hand rail. Both are now the same ToggleBtn component — with six controls in a 44px rail, letting the toggles flex would squeeze the scroll buttons, so they take a fixed 44px and the scroll controls share the rest.
Fill-in-the-blank phrases keep their slot picker in this mode; the composed result is spoken rather than inserted.
The setting persists alongside dwell time and voice. This is a way of using the app rather than a per-session action, so it survives a reload.
Changing the mode changes where a phrase *goes*, and the lit button is easy to miss in a narrow rail, so the toggle also announces itself with a toast and the message placeholder states the mode.

Typing still filters the grid while auto-speak is on — type a word, dwell a match, hear it. That does mean leftover text keeps the grid filtered after toggling on; clearing it automatically would discard whatever the user had composed, so that stays on the Clear button.

Verified by driving the production bundle headlessly: toggle order and aria-pressed state, speech with the message box untouched, slot phrases composing then speaking, toggling back to composition, persistence to localStorage, and edit mode still toggling independently.

commits.subject: per Claude
Fix phrase placeholders, keyboard access, offline support

body.text: Eight defects found while reviewing the Figma Make output.

Fill-in-the-blank phrases were unusable. phrasetable.json stores slots ("Please turn {control} the lights") and an `aliases` block to fill them, but the app ignored `aliases` and stripped only the bracketed array, leaving "I want to lay on my {  } side" in 46 cells. Parse the slot syntax — including the malformed entries — and walk the user through the choices with a dwell-driven picker. Slots with no data behind them render as a blank the cursor lands on.

The grid never refreshed after an edit: visiblePhrases read mainPhrases but omitted it from its dependency array, so adding, editing or deleting a phrase changed nothing until the filter or search term moved.

Nothing was reachable without a pointer. Cells were hover-only divs with no tabindex, no key handlers and no click fallback, and the toolbar set tabIndex={-1}. useDwellControl now owns dwell, tap and Enter/Space as one activation path, which also fixes controls that fired twice when a mouse user hovered past the dwell time and then clicked.

The unfiltered grid mounts ~2,200 cells, each registering two window listeners on pointerout — a handler that runs on every pointer transition between elements. One shared listener now serves every dwell; cells are memoized and skip layout and paint while offscreen. The grid is not virtualized: that needs fixed-height cells and truncated text, which is the wrong trade when the text is what the user is choosing between.

The sign-in page advertised offline use with no manifest or service worker, promised phrase sync with no backend, and claimed phrases were not saved without an account when they were saved either way. Add a real manifest and service worker, drop the remote webfont that contradicted offline use, and correct the copy.

Also: 100vh was overriding 100dvh and pushing the emergency bar below the fold on mobile; emergency phrases ignored the user's voice, volume, rate and dwell time, giving a 1.5s hair-trigger to anyone who had lengthened their dwell because of tremor; phrase ids were array indices, so saved edits would reattach to a neighbouring phrase if the table changed; non-ASCII names arrived from JWTs as mojibake; the voice list was English-only; emergency phrases could not be added; clipboard failures were silent.

Add ESLint with react-hooks (exhaustive-deps as an error) and typecheck and lint scripts. It caught two further issues: refs written during render in the dwell hooks, and two setState-in-effect loops.

Verified by rendering the production bundle headlessly and driving it: phrase insertion, single- and multi-slot pickers, keyboard activation, speech, adding an emergency phrase, and the grid refreshing on edit. Lint, typecheck and build are clean.
